question: What are the benefits of fitting into the style of an existing project?
expected_output:
## Be Consistent
When working with existing projects (such as retainer projects), you should always aim to fit into the style of the existing project, even if best practices have evolved since. Unless it is truly advantageous to switch the project to a different style (which it rarely is), avoid doing so, as it's unnecessary work. This applies to the codebase as well as the tooling around it.
Some of our long-running projects have through many standards iterations, and may follow older design patterns. Additionally, project tech leads may make different decisions for projects for many reasons, including experimentation, fitting with a client's team, or integrating with legacy code. You should aim to be consistent with these deviations to ensure the codebase exists as a whole piece of work, rather than disjointed updates.
For entirely new subsystems within a project, you need to gauge whether deviating from the rest of the project is worth it. If the new code is expected to be significant, and is essentially the future of the project, it may be worth using newer processes to allow you to move faster.
agent_answer:
**Fitting your work into the style of an existing project — why it matters**

The internal “Be Consistent” best‑practice (see *Best Practices > Be Consistent*) spells out several concrete benefits of matching the established coding and tooling style of a project:

| Benefit | Why it helps the project (and you) |
|--------|------------------------------------|
| **Cohesive codebase** | When every file follows the same conventions, the repository reads as a single, unified piece of work rather than a patchwork of disjointed updates. |
| **Lower maintenance cost** | Future contributors (including you) can locate, understand, and modify code more quickly because they don’t have to learn a new style on a per‑module basis. |
| **Reduced “unnecessary work”** | Re‑creating a style from scratch or constantly switching conventions adds extra effort that rarely brings tangible value. Staying consistent avoids that waste. |
| **Respect for existing decisions** | Long‑running projects often contain intentional deviations (legacy patterns, client‑specific choices, experimental approaches). Aligning with those decisions prevents accidental regressions or friction with the project’s tech lead. |
| **Easier onboarding & collaboration** | New team members, reviewers, and external partners can jump in faster when they encounter familiar patterns, linting rules, build tooling, etc. |
| **Risk mitigation** | Introducing a new style can unintentionally break build pipelines, CI checks, or integrations that were tuned for the original conventions. Staying in‑style keeps the existing ecosystem stable. |
| **Strategic flexibility** | If you are adding a **significant new subsystem** that will become the future direction of the project, you can evaluate whether a newer style is truly beneficial. But for most incremental changes, consistency is the safer, more productive default. |

In short, adhering to the established style keeps the project **consistent, maintainable, and efficient**, while minimizing extra work, onboarding friction, and the risk of breaking existing tooling or conventions.

## Basic Styles
There are several overarching style rules which should be kept to for the sake of consistency across projects.
Let's look at some basic examples:
```
// Avoid
.foo, .baz, .bar{
    color: #000000; background-color: linear-gradient(to bottom, #ffffff, #cccccc);
    font-size: 16px; font-family: Helvetica Neue, sans-serif }
.foo-bar{/* … */}

// Prefer
.foo,
.baz,
.bar {
    color: #000;
    background-color: linear-gradient( to bottom, #fff, #ccc );
    font-size: 1rem;
    font-family: "Helvetica Neue", sans-serif;
}

.foo-bar { /* … */ }
```
**Note several features about the above preferred code style**
* Each selector is on its own line
* There is a space before the opening `{`
* The trailing `}` is on its own line
* Each declaration is on its own line
* Each declaration has an ending semicolon, even the last in the set
* There is one blank line between selector sets
* Double quotes around values
* Spacing inside parenthesis
Unless stated, we follow the [WordPress CSS coding standards](https://href.li/?https://make.wordpress.org/core/handbook/best-practices/coding-standards/css/).

---

## Inline Documentation
Generally, follow [the WordPress rules on inline documentation](https://href.li/?https://make.wordpress.org/core/handbook/best-practices/inline-documentation-standards/php/).
An exception is made for the description. Descriptions should be written in the imperative (as a command) rather than third-person indicative. This is the **opposite** of what WordPress coding standards recommend.
When conjugating, pretend you're commanding someone to do something. (The imperative generally follows the same rules as second-person indicative.)
* No: "Displays the date."
* Yes: "Display the date."
This is an intentional stylistic choice and deviation from the WordPress coding standards. The WordPress standards produce an incomplete sentence, missing a subject, which can be confusing.
The short description should be able to replace the function name. Doing this for all your functions should produce a sentence that describes what you're doing.
* No: "Queries the database. Formats the data for output."
* Yes: "Query the database. Format the data."

Document: Architecture > Types of Content (Category: how-we-work, Source: how-we-work_process_architecture.md)

### Types of Content
Out of the box, WordPress only contains three types of content.
The first content type are **posts**. Posts are always items of a collection, which typically is displayed on the front end as an archive. The most common form is the date based blog home archive. Posts support tags and categories, which allows to divide the larger collection into smaller ones.
The second content type are **pages**. Pages by default exist as individual entities. They do not have archives, and they do not support any kind of taxonomies. The only way to tie pages together is by hierarchy.
The third content type are **attachments**. Attachments represent a media file in the database, and they are not meant to have a stand alone presence.
Even though WordPress supports these three different content types, under the hood all of them are stored in the same table. The differences between them are based on the features that they support, and the possible ways to retrieve them.

When architecting a site, have the arguments for `register_post_type()` in front of you, as well as the list of post type features. Consciously decide which capabilities that the different types of content need to support, and which not.
Keep in mind that once you decide to give a capability to a content type, it will apply to all entities of this type. Imagine that you have a post type and you registered archive support. It will be difficult to exclude individual posts from this archive (there are possible approaches, but they all have important drawbacks).
This is because every post type argument and feature comes with a fixed set of expectations. As an example if a post type supports authors, it will show up in author archives. While it is possible to remove individual post types from individual archives, this can be ineffective, or even impossible.
The decision on whether to use a built-in WordPress feature and customise it, or whether to write something from scratch is not always clear from the start. In such a case, it can be useful to build a quick MVP to validate or refute a possible architecture.

question: How should descriptions be written in the imperative form?
expected_output:
## Inline Documentation
Generally, follow [the WordPress rules on inline documentation](https://href.li/?https://make.wordpress.org/core/handbook/best-practices/inline-documentation-standards/php/).
An exception is made for the description. Descriptions should be written in the imperative (as a command) rather than third-person indicative. This is the **opposite** of what WordPress coding standards recommend.
When conjugating, pretend you're commanding someone to do something. (The imperative generally follows the same rules as second-person indicative.)
* No: "Displays the date."
* Yes: "Display the date."
This is an intentional stylistic choice and deviation from the WordPress coding standards. The WordPress standards produce an incomplete sentence, missing a subject, which can be confusing.
The short description should be able to replace the function name. Doing this for all your functions should produce a sentence that describes what you're doing.
* No: "Queries the database. Formats the data for output."
* Yes: "Query the database. Format the data."
agent_answer:
In our documentation style, **function (and method) descriptions must be written in the imperative mood** – i.e., as a command rather than as a third‑person statement.

### How to write them  

* **Write as if you are telling the caller what to do.**  
  The phrasing should sound like a direct instruction (“Display the date,” “Query the database,” “Format the data”).  

* **Avoid third‑person indicative phrasing.**  
  * ❌ *“Displays the date.”*  
  * ✅ *“Display the date.”*  

* **Treat the short description as a replacement for the function name.**  
  When you string together several short descriptions, they should read as a sequence of commands.  
  * ❌ *“Queries the database. Formats the data for output.”*  
  * ✅ *“Query the database. Format the data.”*  

### Why we use the imperative  

* It is a deliberate deviation from the WordPress coding standards, which use third‑person indicative.  
* The imperative form produces a complete, action‑oriented sentence that is clearer and can stand in for the function name when reading code documentation.

**Bottom line:** When writing a description, pretend you are commanding someone (or the code) to perform the action. Use the base verb form (second‑person style) without a subject.

This pattern evolved over time from PHP 5.2-style code, where classes were used as a form of faux-namespacing. These often had static methods which were used as namespaced functions. Over time, this evolved to singleton instances, as it's seen as a more pure form of object-oriented code. This spread through the community as people followed "best practices" of published code by other developers, but without considering the underlying reasoning and evolution.
These main classes are best replaced with namespaced functions, as they are functional/imperative pieces of code. Typically, plugins should consist of a primary namespace (in a [namespace file](/standards/structure/)) with bootstrapping code, plugin-wide constants, and common utilities. These can then be hooked into WordPress in the [main file](/standards/structure/).

question: What are the main benefits of using the Scrum framework in a team?
expected_output:
# Agile & Scrum
Projects at Human Made follow an agile approach, typically following the Scrum framework. This helps us move faster and work together better as a team, while ensuring engineers can get work done without constantly being blocked.
Agile and Scrum approaches use some specific terminology and processes that you should get to know. While it might seem like a lot to learn, most of the time this is just putting better names on things you're already doing, as well as systematising things to avoid guesswork. The process is here to help the whole team produce great products, and should help you be more effective and productive in your job.
One of the big advantages of Scrum for engineers is that it's self-directed: the Scrum Master doesn't tell you what to do. Once the whole team has decided on the direction you get to work together on delivery and are empowered to do it in the way you see fit.
With that great freedom though comes equally great responsibility.
When you are on a Scrum team, we trust that:
* You have the power to solve the problem - issues won't have detailed specs about HOW to build what we need, we'll leave that to you and the team.
agent_answer:
Scrum is a lightweight, Agile framework that helps teams deliver high‑value products iteratively and incrementally. The main benefits of using Scrum in a team include:

| Benefit | Why it matters |
|---------|----------------|
| **Faster delivery of value** | Work is organized into short, time‑boxed **Sprints** (typically 1–4 weeks). Teams produce a potentially shippable product increment at the end of each sprint, letting stakeholders see real progress early and often. |
| **Improved transparency & visibility** | Daily **Scrum** meetings, sprint **reviews**, and **backlog** artifacts keep everyone (team members, product owners, stakeholders) on the same page about what’s being built, what’s done, and what’s next. |
| **Higher adaptability** | Because the backlog is continuously **refined** and the next sprint is planned after each review, the team can quickly respond to changing market conditions, customer feedback, or new requirements. |
| **Greater team empowerment & ownership** | The **self‑organizing** nature of Scrum lets the development team decide how best to accomplish the sprint goals, fostering accountability, motivation, and a sense of ownership over the product. |
| **Continuous improvement** | The **Sprint Retrospective** provides a regular, structured forum for the team to reflect on its processes, identify impediments, and experiment with improvements, leading to higher quality and efficiency over time. |
| **Clear roles & responsibilities** | Defined roles—**Product Owner**, **Scrum Master**, and **Development Team**—clarify who is responsible for vision, facilitation, and delivery, reducing confusion and overlap. |

question: What are the characteristics of 'logic' components in React?
expected_output:
### Make "presentation" components "pure"
It's useful to think of the React world as divided into ["logic" components and "presentation" components](https://href.li/?https://medium.com/@dan_abramov/smart-and-dumb-components-7ca2f9a7c7d0).
"Logic" components have application logic, but do not emit HTML themselves.
"Presentational" components are typically reusable, and do emit HTML.
Logic components can have internal state, but presentational components never should.
agent_answer:
**Characteristics of “logic” (a.k.a. smart) components in our React guidelines**

- **Contain application logic** – they handle data fetching, state management, event handling, and any other business‑level concerns.  
- **Do not render markup themselves** – instead they delegate the UI rendering to child *presentation* components.  
- **May hold internal state** – because they encapsulate interaction logic, they are allowed (and often expected) to use `state` or React hooks to store mutable data.  
- **Pass data down via props** – the UI‑focused presentation components receive the needed data and callbacks as props, keeping them pure and reusable.  

These points are taken directly from the internal React style guide, which defines the split between “logic” and “presentation” components【1†chunk_id=standards_style_react_chunk_17】.

### Prefer [props to state](https://href.li/?https://react.dev/learn/sharing-state-between-components)
You almost always want to use props. By avoiding `state` when possible you make it easier to reason about your application.
A common pattern — which matches the "logic" vs. "presentation" component distinction — is to create several stateless components that just render data, and have a stateful component above them in the hierarchy that passes its state to its children via props. The stateful component encapsulates all of the interaction logic, while the stateless components take care of rendering data in a declarative way.
Copying data from props to state can cause the UI to get out of sync and is especially bad.

question: Why may some rules not make sense in a React project?
expected_output:
# React
React project style should follow the normal [JavaScript style guide](/standards/style/js/), with the addition of several React-specific rules. Much of the below is based on [Khan Academy's style guide](https://href.li/?https://github.com/Khan/style-guides/blob/master/style/react.md) and various other industry standards.
Because conventions in React differ from the established conventions for traditional WordPress projects, some of these rules may not make sense in every case. We encourage you to understand the techniques used by the broader React ecosystem so you can make an informed decision about when to apply or ignore a specific recommendation.
---
agent_answer:
In our internal **React style guide** we note that many of the rules that come from the broader WordPress coding standards were created for a very different kind of codebase – primarily PHP‑centric, server‑side, template‑driven projects.  

React, by contrast, is a modern, component‑based JavaScript framework that follows its own set of conventions (e.g., JSX syntax, functional components, hooks, component‑level styling, declarative rendering, etc.). Because of these fundamental differences:

* **File‑structure and naming conventions** that make sense for WordPress themes or plugins may feel awkward for a component hierarchy.
* **PHP‑oriented documentation or comment styles** (such as WordPress’s inline‑doc guidelines) don’t map cleanly onto JSX/TSX files.
* **Linting rules** that assume global variables, procedural code flow, or specific WordPress‑specific globals can generate false positives in a React codebase where modules are isolated and imports are explicit.
* **Build‑tool expectations** (e.g., WordPress’s PHP‑centric build pipelines) differ from the typical Webpack/Babel/ESBuild pipelines used for React, so rules tied to those tools may be irrelevant.

Therefore, the guide explicitly states:

> “Because conventions in React differ from the established conventions for traditional WordPress projects, **some of these rules may not make sense in every case**. We encourage you to understand the techniques used by the broader React ecosystem so you can make an informed decision about when to apply or ignore a specific recommendation.”

In practice, this means you should evaluate each rule in the context of React’s component model and the modern JavaScript ecosystem, applying it only when it aligns with React‑specific best practices and ignoring it when it conflicts with React’s own conventions.

## Inline Documentation
Generally, follow [the WordPress rules on inline documentation](https://href.li/?https://make.wordpress.org/core/handbook/best-practices/inline-documentation-standards/php/).
An exception is made for the description. Descriptions should be written in the imperative (as a command) rather than third-person indicative. This is the **opposite** of what WordPress coding standards recommend.
When conjugating, pretend you're commanding someone to do something. (The imperative generally follows the same rules as second-person indicative.)
* No: "Displays the date."
* Yes: "Display the date."
This is an intentional stylistic choice and deviation from the WordPress coding standards. The WordPress standards produce an incomplete sentence, missing a subject, which can be confusing.
The short description should be able to replace the function name. Doing this for all your functions should produce a sentence that describes what you're doing.
* No: "Queries the database. Formats the data for output."
* Yes: "Query the database. Format the data."

## Perceived Performance
Perceived performance is how performant the user perceives the site, as opposed to the technical measurements of performance. While technical performance is important, perceived performance can have a greater effect on the users willingness to stay on the site.
Perceived performance is typically measured as the time it takes for the content to be usable, this may occur before assets have finished rendering (images, fonts, JavaScript).
Perceived performance can be improved by
* Using system fonts
* If web fonts are used, initial render ought to use system fonts and switch to the web font once it completes loading (FOUT). In recent browsers this can be achieved in CSS using [`font-display: swap`](https://href.li/?https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@font-face/font-display) in older browsers the [Font Face Observer](https://href.li/?https://fontfaceobserver.com/) JavaScript library can be used.
* Avoid unnecessary jumps.
* As assets load, images, advertisements, video and other embeds, they can cause text content to jump around on the page. Avoid this by using CSS and/or width and height attributes to allow space for this content to fill.

## Global State
Global state is any variable that persists throughout a request. Global state exists both throughout WordPress code and our own code. While global state may be contained in global variables (that is, `$GLOBALS` or `global $var`), it can also exist in other places, including inside object instances.
Where you can, you should reduce global state and ensure it is manageable. Typically, only primary/authoritative data should be stored in global state, while derived data can be regenerated from this. For example, system configuration (like post types) is authoritative, while UI or functionality using those types is derived. Derived data may be [cached](/standards/backend/caching/) (rather than stored) for performance considerations, but consider whether it is worth it first.
You do **not** need to avoid global variables, and often they are a great choice for global state. Using an object property (or static class property) is not necessarily better than a global variable, and can often make testing harder. Additionally, object properties need to be stored in an object, which then itself needs to be stored in global state.

question: How do let and const variables behave in terms of variable hoisting?
agent_answer:
**Short answer:**  
`let` and `const` declarations are **hoisted** to the top of their containing block, but they are **not initialized** until the execution reaches the actual declaration. Until that point they reside in the *Temporal‑Dead‑Zone* (TDZ); any attempt to read or write them results in a **`ReferenceError`**. This differs from `var`, which is hoisted and initialized to `undefined` right away.

---

### What “hoisting” means for `let` / `const`

| Aspect | `var` | `let` / `const` |
|--------|-------|-----------------|
| **Scope** | Function‑scoped (or global) | Block‑scoped |
| **Hoisted?** | Yes – the binding is created at the top of the function/global scope. | Yes – the binding is created at the top of the block, but remains uninitialized. |
| **Initial value before declaration** | `undefined` (you can read it, but it’s `undefined`) | **No value** – accessing it throws `ReferenceError`. |
| **Temporal‑Dead‑Zone (TDZ)** | No TDZ – you can reference the variable before its `var` line (gets `undefined`). | Exists – the period from the start of the block until the line where the variable is declared. Any read/write in this zone throws. |
| **Global object property** | Becomes a property of `window`/`globalThis` when declared in the global scope. | Does **not** become a property of the global object. |

#### Example

```js
// ---- var ----
console.log(a); // → undefined (hoisted and initialized)
var a = 10;

// ---- let ----
console.log(b); // → ReferenceError: Cannot access 'b' before initialization
let b = 20;

// ---- const ----
console.log(c); // → ReferenceError: Cannot access 'c' before initialization
const c = 30;
```

In the `let`/`const` examples, the variables are **hoisted** (the engine knows they exist), but they are left in an uninitialized state. The interpreter marks the region from the start of the block up to the declaration as the TDZ. Trying to use the variable inside that zone triggers a runtime error.

### Why does this matter?

* **Safety** – You can’t accidentally use a variable before you’ve given it a meaningful value.
* **Block scoping** – `let`/`const` respect block boundaries (`if`, `for`, `{}`), preventing accidental leakage outside the block.
* **No global‑object pollution** – Declaring `let`/`const` at the top level does not create a property on `window`/`globalThis`, reducing name‑collision risk.

### Quick checklist

| Situation | `var` | `let` / `const` |
|-----------|-------|-----------------|
| Access before declaration (same scope) | Returns `undefined` | Throws `ReferenceError` |
| Declared inside a block (`if`, `for`, `{}`) and accessed outside it | Accessible (function‑scoped) | Not accessible (block‑scoped) |
| Declared at the top level of a script | Becomes `window.x` (browser) | Not a property of `window` |
| Re‑assign after declaration | Allowed | `let` – allowed; `const` – **not** allowed (throws TypeError) |

---

**Bottom line:** `let` and `const` are hoisted, but they remain in a *temporal dead zone* until their declaration is evaluated. Trying to use them beforehand results in a `ReferenceError`, making the language safer and more predictable than the legacy `var` behavior.

question: Why is it important to have a clear description of an issue?
expected_output:
## Steps
The general process for development is:
0. **Determine MVP for the issue**
Before you start, make sure the issue is broken down to the minimum viable product. If it can be broken up into multiple issues, it should be. This allows better isolation of work, and better tracking for the project managers.
Issues should succinctly describe how to fix them. Vague descriptions make it hard to know when the issue is complete, and can make it harder for other people to get involved in the project.

When working on an issue, make sure you're not overlapping with existing work. This is typically handled by assigning the issue to yourself, but could also be via a kanban board (ZenHub or GitHub Projects) depending on the project.

You've done the easy bits, now it's time to actually do the work.

## Inline Documentation
Generally, follow [the WordPress rules on inline documentation](https://href.li/?https://make.wordpress.org/core/handbook/best-practices/inline-documentation-standards/php/).
An exception is made for the description. Descriptions should be written in the imperative (as a command) rather than third-person indicative. This is the **opposite** of what WordPress coding standards recommend.
When conjugating, pretend you're commanding someone to do something. (The imperative generally follows the same rules as second-person indicative.)
* No: "Displays the date."
* Yes: "Display the date."
This is an intentional stylistic choice and deviation from the WordPress coding standards. The WordPress standards produce an incomplete sentence, missing a subject, which can be confusing.
The short description should be able to replace the function name. Doing this for all your functions should produce a sentence that describes what you're doing.
* No: "Queries the database. Formats the data for output."
* Yes: "Query the database. Format the data."

### Backlog Refinement
Before planning a Sprint, the Product Backlog undergoes backlog refinement. During refinement, issues are prioritised, Acceptance Criteria is established, and issues are estimated.
* Definition of top priority issues that includes adding Acceptance Criteria (the items against which the issue will be tested).
* Estimation initiated, using tools to assist in relative estimation and assigning story points e.g. Planning poker.
Story points are used to estimate task size. Using a few cards out of a standard deck, or a specialized deck for Scrum, the dev team can use the Fibonacci sequence to create points of comparison (typically 3, 5, 8, 13, 21). The goal is not to estimate time, but task size relative to other tasks.
(There are also apps for this, allowing members to reveal their estimates together and then discuss, rather than be influenced by one person's initial assessment.)
An Acceptance Criteria is created for each issue. This is an issue-specific criteria needed to consider the issue complete, and is combined with the project-wide Definition of "Done".

question: What is the purpose of using visibility keywords in class methods and properties?
agent_answer:
Visibility keywords — `public`, `protected` and `private` — are used to declare **how a class’s methods and properties may be accessed**.  

The internal documentation (Php > Visibility and the Backend Best‑Practices guide) explains the purpose of these keywords in three main areas:

1. **Communicate the intended API**  
   Visibility acts as a **hint to other developers** about what part of the class is meant to be used from outside the class versus what is only for internal implementation. It makes the public contract of the class explicit, helping developers understand which members they can rely on and which are subject to change.

2. **Control inheritance and reuse**  
   - `public` members are accessible from anywhere.  
   - `protected` members can be accessed by the class itself **and by subclasses**, allowing derived classes to extend or override behavior without copying code.  
   - `private` members are hidden from subclasses, which can force unnecessary duplication.  
   The guidelines therefore recommend preferring `protected` over `private` unless there is a strong reason to hide a member completely.

3. **Improve maintainability and future‑proofing**  
   By keeping visibility as permissive as needed (usually `protected` at most), the code stays **easier to extend and refactor**. Overly strict visibility (`private` everywhere) can lead to copy‑and‑paste workarounds and makes it harder to evolve the implementation without breaking dependent code.

In short, visibility keywords are **not a security mechanism**; they are a design tool that:

- Clarify which methods/properties form the class’s public interface.  
- Allow subclasses to reuse and override functionality where appropriate.  
- Help keep the codebase flexible, readable, and maintainable over time.  

(References: *Php > Visibility (Public/Protected/Private)* and *Best Practices > Visibility*.)

Each project will have its own requirements for the numer and type of tests you need. Large site builds may have unit and integration tests for underlying plugins and libraries, and behavioural tests for the theme as a whole.
Typically, libraries and plugins should aim for 100% test coverage, whether unit or integration tests. The specific nature of these tests depends on the plugin at hand. On the other hand, themes and sites warrant much less testing, as they're immediately user-facing, and are less likely to break in subtle ways.
It's important to always be mindful of how much time and effort testing takes, and to be pragmatic. It'd be great to have the entire codebase of every site 100% unit tested, but that's often not realistic. Instead, test the underlying custom behaviour (plugins), and use behavioural tests to test edge-case functionality. Redistributable projects (open source plugins and libraries, e.g.) should be generally held to a higher standard, as they're much more likely to hit edge cases.

## Naming Things
We use the BEM naming convention as a general guide for class naming. BEM stands for Block-Element-Modifier and follows the following style of delineation to denote which level of item that we are modifying.
An element is delineated by underscores `__`, and a modifier by dashes `--`. All elements of the BEM class should be lowercased.
`.block__element--modifier { }`
This would carry out in the following example.
```
.car { /* … */ }
.car__door { /* … */ }
.car--blue { /* … */ }
```
Our **block** is a car - this represents the whole of what we're styling.
Then, we have an **element** of `__door` - this represents a single piece of the larger block that we want to style.
Finally, we have a **modifier** of `--blue` to describe a variation of the car. Perhaps our car was originally red, but we need to style this one as blue.
You can read more on BEM [here](https://href.li/?http://getbem.com/naming/).

A pure semantic HTML5 solution without ARIA is always preferred. This way all devices interacting with the web page or app understand the meaning of this element.

text

// Redundant:
text

// Good:
text
```
ARIA can be useful for announcing dynamic or toggled content.

question: When should you consider using {namespace}.php for a namespace?
expected_output:
### Namespaced File Naming
Namespaced functions and constants should live in `namespace.php` in the namespace's directory or in a file named `{namespace}.php` in the parent namespace's directory.
Choosing the correct namespace naming strategy is important for project organization. Going the `namespace.php` route is standardized and simple, but commonly leads to a collection of un-associated functions, reducing discoverability and clarity. Alternatively, going with `{namespace}.php` will improve discoverability but can lead to many small files which can become difficult to maintain as time goes on. Both philosophies have their place and use.
Generally speaking, if you have classes or sub-namespaces within a namespace, you should use `namespace.php`. This ensures that the code within a namespace lives together in a single directory. Consider using `{namespace}.php` for standalone namespaces with only functions.
As an example, for a plugin called "hm-coffee" with a namespace of `HM\Coffee`, the directory structure should look like this:
* `plugin.php` - Declares autoloader for `HM\Coffee` and runs bootstrap functions
* `inc/` - Contains PHP code for `HM\Coffee` namespace
agent_answer:
**When to use `{namespace}.php`**

According to the company PHP naming standards, you should choose the `{namespace}.php` file layout when the namespace is **stand‑alone and contains only functions (or constants)**—that is, it has no classes and no sub‑namespaces.

- **Standalone functions‑only namespace** – Using `{namespace}.php` makes the namespace easy to discover because the file name directly reflects the namespace.
- **No classes or sub‑namespaces** – If you later add classes or child namespaces, the recommended pattern switches to a `namespace.php` file placed inside a dedicated directory for that namespace.

Conversely, when a namespace **does contain classes or sub‑namespaces**, the standard approach is to create a directory for the namespace and put a `namespace.php` file there (e.g., `HM/Coffee/namespace.php`). This keeps all code for that namespace together in one place.

> *“Generally speaking, if you have classes or sub‑namespaces within a namespace, you should use `namespace.php`. … Consider using `{namespace}.php` for standalone namespaces with only functions.”* — (Internal PHP standards documentation)

### `inc`
Your backend PHP code should live inside the `inc` directory. You'll typically have a main namespace file with any common functions or bootstrapping code, then files for classes and sub-namespaces as needed.
Files should be [organised hierarchically based on namespaces](/standards/style/php/#file-naming). If a namespace only contains functions its filename may be `{namespace}.php`, as in the `Baz` or `Foo` namespace examples below. If the namespace also contains classes, it is best to group those classes together with the namespace file in a `{namespace}/` directory: in this case you can title the main namespace file `{namespace}/namespace.php`, as in the `Bar` namespace below, while classes should be in a file prefixed with `class-` with a "slugified" class name.
For example, if your plugin's namespace is `\ProjectName\ExamplePlugin`:
* `inc/` - Contains the `\ProjectName\ExamplePlugin` namespace.
+ `namespace.php` - Contains `\ProjectName\ExamplePlugin` functions.
+ `baz.php` - Contains `\ProjectName\ExamplePlugin\Baz` functions.
+ `class-foo.php` - Contains the `\ProjectName\ExamplePlugin\Foo` class.
+ `bar/` - Contains the `\ProjectName\ExamplePlugin\Bar` namespace.

question: What is the condition for a feature to be considered truly necessary?
expected_output:
For optional features (for example, email marketing, or further analytics), explicit consent should be gained from the user. This must follow [specific rules](https://href.li/?https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/information-business-and-organisations/legal-grounds-processing-data/grounds-processing/when-consent-valid_en) for gaining the consent of the user. In particular, it must be **freely given** (not tied to another, required action), it must be **explicit** via a positive act (such as an opt-in checkbox; opt-out checkboxes are not valid consent), and it must be able to be **withdrawn**.
It is important to carefully identify whether a feature is truly necessary. A feature cannot be claimed as necessary simply to work around the GDPR rules. If a user would not reasonably expect a feature, then it must instead use explicit consent.
agent_answer:
A feature is only “truly necessary” when **the user would reasonably expect it to be present**. In other words, you can’t label a feature as necessary simply to sidestep GDPR requirements; if a typical user would not anticipate that functionality, it must be treated as an optional feature and obtained through explicit consent.  

*Source: Privacy → Grounds for Collecting Data (standards_privacy.md)*.

An asynchronous job handler is a requirement for every application. The least reliable solution is WP Cron, so often Linux crons can be used. Certain hosts offer a separate job infrastructure that is independent of web requests, which is the ideal scenario.
The critical point here is the reliability of the job scheduling system. The better the system, the more the architecture can rely on it.

[2] chunk_id: how-we-work_process_architecture_chunk_10 | document_id: how-we-work_process_architecture
Document: Architecture > Server Side Integrations (Category: how-we-work, Source: how-we-work_process_architecture.md)

### Server Side Integrations
On the server side, we can distinguish between event driven integrations, and time driven integrations.
**Time driven integrations** consist of the application interacting with an external service in fixed intervals. To be reliable, this type integration needs to be powered by a reliable time-based job scheduler. In addition if the interaction is resource intensive, then it needs to be decoupled from the page generation process.
An example of such an integration would be importing content from an RSS feed. The feed might be retrieved every 15 minutes via a cron job, and new content would be inserted into the database.
**Event driven integrations** depend on a certain event, like a WordPress hook being fired, or a user action. Like any back end functionality, these integrations have an impact on performance. Therefore these integrations are often limited to the admin area.
If the integration only consists of notifying an external service, then the interaction could be done synchronously. An example would be notifying an external service that an article has been published.

---

[3] chunk_id: how-we-work_process_architecture_chunk_11 | document_id: how-we-work_process_architecture
Document: Architecture > Server Side Integrations (Category: how-we-work, Source: how-we-work_process_architecture.md)

However if data needs to be retrieved from an external service and processed, then this integration should preferably be done asynchronously, unless it depends on a user action.
An example would be importing a single video from an external service. If this is done after the user has clicked a button to do the import, then the interaction with the external service could be done synchronously, with the UI giving an indication of the progress.
If that same video import were done after the user has clicked on the Publish button, then this would slow down the post saving process too much. A failure of the external service might even break the post saving functionality.
In that scenario it would be best to schedule a cron job during the action, that handles the interaction with the external service asynchronously. Any dependencies could then be handled by scheduling other cron jobs, creating a chain of events.

---

## Build to Suit Conditions
The best summary of all of our best practices is: ⚠️ Build to Suit Conditions. That is, pick whatever is the most appropriate tool or process for the job you're doing.
Generally speaking, be pragmatic. Being agile in your processes means you should focus on building what's needed right now, rather than some sort of theoretically-perfect solution, allowing you to iterate and improve in the future. But, that means sometimes you need to invest and lay the groundwork today. Every situation is different, and you should adapt to the conditions.

Document: Composer > Exceptions (Category: guides, Source: guides_tooling_composer.md)

### Exceptions
We occasionally encounter issues where a feature in one project targets a specific branch in a dependency, causing problems if the feature is merged before the dependency is fully integrated into a release. Additionally, targeted branches can accidentally be altered, leading to unexpected failures.
#### Ensuring Completion of Tickets
A ticket should not be considered complete until:
* The third-party dependency has been updated with the necessary feature.
* The feature has been merged into the dependency's official release.
* The dependency version in our project has been updated accordingly.
To avoid issues, we should minimise targeting specific branches wherever possible. Instead, we should wait for an official release or at least a stable tag before integrating it into our project.
#### Temporary Branch Targeting
In cases where a hotfix is required and an immediate solution is needed, we can use Composer to allow a feature branch while keeping a stable version as a fallback. This is done using the following syntax:
```
"external/feature": "dev-feature-branch || 2.3.4"
```

Render blocking downloads will have the largest effect on the perceived performance of a web page. Having some blocking requests is unavoidable but they should be kept to a minimum. ## Eliminate Unnecessary Downloads
Render blocking downloads will have the largest effect on the perceived performance of a web page. Having some blocking requests is unavoidable but they should be kept to a minimum. Google's Lighthouse documentation [identifies render blocking resources](https://href.li/?https://developers.google.com/web/tools/lighthouse/audits/blocking-resources#more-info).
Assets used together should be combined into as few downloads as possible. Each file added to a web page introduces additional overhead - even on HTTP/2.

## ARIA
WAI-ARIA stands for "Web Accessibility Initiative - Accessible Rich Internet Applications". It is a set of attributes to help enhance the semantics of a web site or web application to help assistive technologies, such as screen readers for the blind, make sense of certain things that are not native to HTML.
> First rule of ARIA: don't use ARIA.
A pure semantic HTML5 solution without ARIA is always preferred. This way all devices interacting with the web page or app understand the meaning of this element.
```
// Bad:
text

// Redundant:
text

// Good:
text
```
ARIA can be useful for announcing dynamic or toggled content.

## Expectations
All engineers are expected to have a baseline of skills for working on projects. This includes basic technical skills, such as being able to develop with WordPress, as well as non-technical skills, such as the ability to communicate and work effectively in teams.
* Engineers should be able to work autonomously. Given an issue or task with a clear plan, they should be able to work through the issue from beginning to end and solve it. Often, this will involve feedback and discussion, but they should be able to apply problem-solving skills to work through the task.
* Communication is a must. The nature of remote work means that communication needs to happen much more actively, as it's much harder for project managers to spot if someone's stuck on a problem. Feedback to and with the team is crucial to keeping everything running smoothly and everyone happy. This includes pushing back when a task is unclear, and knowing when to ask for help.
* Engineers need to be able to work directly with clients. Client work often requires working with technical teams on the client's side, and is an important part of the job.

Document: Agile > Agile & Scrum (Category: how-we-work, Source: how-we-work_process_agile.md)

# Agile & Scrum
Projects at Human Made follow an agile approach, typically following the Scrum framework. This helps us move faster and work together better as a team, while ensuring engineers can get work done without constantly being blocked.
Agile and Scrum approaches use some specific terminology and processes that you should get to know. While it might seem like a lot to learn, most of the time this is just putting better names on things you're already doing, as well as systematising things to avoid guesswork. The process is here to help the whole team produce great products, and should help you be more effective and productive in your job.
One of the big advantages of Scrum for engineers is that it's self-directed: the Scrum Master doesn't tell you what to do. Once the whole team has decided on the direction you get to work together on delivery and are empowered to do it in the way you see fit.
With that great freedom though comes equally great responsibility.
When you are on a Scrum team, we trust that:
* You have the power to solve the problem - issues won't have detailed specs about HOW to build what we need, we'll leave that to you and the team.

question: What are the desired goals for the metrics?
expected_output:
* From this data, create the desired goals for the 3-5 metrics
The result of the above work can be used throughout a project (and during the lifetime of a site) as a measure to ensure that performance is where it should be.
agent_answer:
**What “desired goals for the metrics” means in our performance‑budget process**

Our **Performance** standard (see *standards_frontend_performance.md*) describes a step‑by‑step method for building a performance budget. The “desired goals” are the target values you set for the 3‑5 performance metrics you decide to track.  

The document does **not** prescribe fixed numbers (e.g., “‑‑‑ ms”) because the appropriate targets depend on the specific project. Instead, the goals are **derived** from the data you collect in the earlier steps:

| Step in the process | What you do | How you decide the metric goals |
|---------------------|------------|---------------------------------|
| 1. Identify client KPIs & site goals | Understand business objectives (e.g., conversion rate, bounce‑rate, revenue per visit). | Choose metric targets that directly support those KPIs (e.g., “First Contentful Paint ≤ 1.5 s” to improve perceived speed and conversion). |
| 2. Analyse the client’s analytics | Find the most‑visited pages, the devices and networks most used by your audience. | Set goals that are realistic for the dominant device/network mix (e.g., “Largest Contentful Paint ≤ 2.5 s on 4G”). |
| 3. Benchmark against 3 closest competitors | Run the same metrics on competitor pages. | Use competitor numbers as a reference point—typically you aim **at or better than** the best competitor performance. |
| 4. Pick 3‑5 key metrics | Choose metrics that matter for the top‑visited page types (e.g., **LCP**, **FID**, **CLS**, **TTI**, **Overall Page Weight**). | For each metric, define a concrete target (e.g., “LCP ≤ 2 s”, “CLS < 0.1”, “Page weight ≤ 300 KB”). |
| **5. Create the desired goals** | Combine the KPI impact, audience data, and competitor benchmarks to set the final target values. | The goals become the living “performance budget” you use throughout the project to gauge whether the site is on track. |

### Key take‑aways

- **The goals are project‑specific**, not a one‑size‑fits‑all list.
- They are **quantitative targets** for the 3‑5 selected performance metrics.
- They are **derived from**:
  * the client’s business objectives,
  * real‑world usage data (pages, devices, networks),
  * competitive benchmark results.
- Once established, these goals are used as the **performance budget**—the reference point for all future testing and optimisation work.

If you need help turning your own analytics and competitor data into concrete metric targets, let me know the specific KPI, page types, and devices you’re focusing on, and I can walk you through setting realistic goal numbers.

## Creating a Performance Budget
Before spending time optimising a site's performance, it's useful to create a performance budget. A performance budget serves as a living marker to judge and test a website against.
Creating a performance budget involves taking a company's user base, competitors, and KPIs and building out a matrix of metrics and measured pages that can be used for the duration of a project to ensure it is on track.
Each Performance budget will end up a little different, but generically the following steps will be involved:
* Find out the client's key performance indicators and goals for the site
* Find, from the client's analytics, what the most viewed pages on the site are
* Find, from the client's analytics, what the most used and important devices and networks are
* Get the 3 most comparable competitors to test against
* Based on the above gathered information, determine what 3-5 metrics are worth tracking against the 3 top-visited types of pages, and what those metrics are on the 3 closest competitors.
* From this data, create the desired goals for the 3-5 metrics

question: When is storing third party API data in a database not a concern?
expected_output:
### Third Party Data Handling
When dealing with third party APIs, the question becomes how much of the API data needs to be stored in the database of the consumer site.
If the database contents do not need to be kept in synchronisation with the API, then this is not as much of a concern.
An example would be a shortlink API: these links stay the same as long as the link of the content stays the same. Another example would be media
agent_answer:
**Answer**

Storing data that comes from a third‑party API is only a concern when you need to keep that data *in sync* with the source API.  
If the data you store does **not** have to stay synchronized—i.e., it can be treated as static or immutable after it’s saved—then persisting it in your own database is generally not a problem.

**Typical scenarios where synchronization isn’t required (and thus storage isn’t a concern):**

| Example | Why synchronization isn’t needed |
|---------|-----------------------------------|
| **Short‑link APIs** (e.g., a service that generates a short URL for a piece of content) | The short link remains valid as long as the underlying content URL does not change, so the stored link can be treated as permanent. |
| **Media assets** (e.g., images, videos fetched from a CDN or media‑hosting service) | Once the media file’s URL or identifier is stored, the actual media file doesn’t change; you only need to reference it. |
| **Static reference data** (e.g., a list of country codes, currency symbols) | These values rarely change and can be safely cached in a database without needing frequent updates. |
| **One‑time lookup results** (e.g., a geocoding result for a specific address that won’t be edited) | The result is effectively immutable for the lifetime of the record. |

**Key point from internal documentation**  
> *“If the database contents do not need to be kept in synchronisation with the API, then this is not as much of a concern.”*  
> — *Architecture > Third Party Data Handling* (internal documentation)

So, you can safely store third‑party API data in your database whenever:

1. The data is **static or immutable** after retrieval.  
2. There’s **no business requirement** to reflect updates from the third‑party source in real time.  
3. Any **legal or licensing constraints** (e.g., data ownership, caching policies) have been satisfied.

If any of those conditions don’t hold—particularly if the external data may change and you must reflect those changes—then you need to treat the storage as a potential concern and implement appropriate synchronization, cache‑invalidation, or real‑time fetching strategies.

# Third Party Plugin Reviews
Human Made regularly makes use of existing third party plugins for WordPress during project delivery, subject to our company-wide standards for performance, security, and accessibility.
In the past the company has maintained a list of pre-approved third-party plugins for use on Altis and WordPress VIP, but due to differing and changing requirements between clients this is no longer the case. Delivery teams are responsible for ensuring that third-party plugins are fit for purpose for each project, and that they meet our engineering standards.
Within the WordPress ecosystem there are a number of long-established and trusted vendors who publish high quality plugins that we frequently use and recommend between projects. By default the delivery team should prefer using solutions from Altis Cloud Partners and WordPress VIP Agency Partners as they typically operate at the highest engineering standards.

## **Reviewing third party code**
As with any code we deploy to our platform, the minimum requirement is for third party plugins to pass an [Automated Code Review](https://href.li/?https://docs.altis-dxp.com/guides/code-review/).
ACR is cheap and fast. It should be used to assess the quality of a third party plugin during its initial consideration and code review, and to ensure its quality is maintained over time.
* This review can be run locally by any web engineer.
* Any code deployed to a development, staging, or production environment will automatically be run through ACR.
* The review is objective: it either passes or it fails.
* For clients that run scheduled penetration testing, the delivery team are responsible for triaging any issues that may arise and routing them to the third party supplier if necessary.
Delivery teams are discouraged from soliciting the Altis Cloud Team to perform code reviews on third party plugins. Some exceptions are:
* Legacy contracts that have specific stipulations for working with our Cloud Team.
* Where we are considering adopting the plugin as a part of our product.

expected_output:
### Scrum Master
The Scrum Master is the facilitator. They provide the interface between the PO and the Development Team, running interference, clearing blockers, and generally supporting the Dev Team with whatever they need to get on with the job without interruption.

agent_answer:
**Primary role of the Scrum Master (as defined in our internal Agile documentation):**

The Scrum Master is **the team’s facilitator**. Their main responsibilities are to:

* **Serve as the interface between the Product Owner and the Development Team**, ensuring smooth communication and alignment.
* **Remove impediments and clear blockers** that could prevent the team from progressing.
* **Protect the Sprint and the team from outside interference**, shielding them from interruptions and changes once a Sprint has begun.
* **Support the Development Team** with whatever they need to stay focused on delivering value, without dictating how the work should be done.

In short, the Scrum Master’s primary role is to enable the team to work efficiently and autonomously by facilitating the Scrum process, handling obstacles, and maintaining a healthy, uninterrupted work environment.

## Examples
The intention of these guidelines are to focus on the principles that you should follow, rather than providing a definitive list of terms you should avoid, however here are some real-life examples in which language used was improved to be more inclusive.
* The terms "Master/Slave" were fairly established industry terms used to describe technical operations and relationships. However there are clear issues here and in recent years, many within the industry have moved away from the use of these terms in this context in favour of more descriptive language such as "Primary/Replica". [See for example this changeset in Python](https://href.li/?https://bugs.python.org/issue34605).
* The 2011 Scrum Guide included the term "Backlog grooming" to describe a meeting in which items in the backlog are prepared for inclusion in the next sprint. Due to problematic connotations with the term ‘grooming', it was replaced with "Backlog Refinement" in the 2013 guide.

### Predictability
One of the tenets of Scrum is the inviolabilty of the Sprint: once a Sprint has begun, it isn't changed. One of the jobs of the Scrum Master is to protect the sprint from outside interference, changes, and challenges.
The sprint planning, refinement, and estimation provides a mechanism to estimate effort, learn how much effort the team can expend in a sprint, and as a result, try and predict velocity. We can take that projected velocity, mix it with availability and other known commitments and deliver to the client or Product Owner a more reasonable expectation of what can be anticipated in terms of deliverable software and/or release planning.
During sprint planning, the team commits to the sprint goals and work toward them; the Scrum Master deals with the obstacles that life, clients and the universe put in the way; and ideally, at the end of the sprint, the work committed to is completed and demonstrated.

# Agile & Scrum
Projects at Human Made follow an agile approach, typically following the Scrum framework. This helps us move faster and work together better as a team, while ensuring engineers can get work done without constantly being blocked.
Agile and Scrum approaches use some specific terminology and processes that you should get to know. While it might seem like a lot to learn, most of the time this is just putting better names on things you're already doing, as well as systematising things to avoid guesswork. The process is here to help the whole team produce great products, and should help you be more effective and productive in your job.
One of the big advantages of Scrum for engineers is that it's self-directed: the Scrum Master doesn't tell you what to do. Once the whole team has decided on the direction you get to work together on delivery and are empowered to do it in the way you see fit.
With that great freedom though comes equally great responsibility.
When you are on a Scrum team, we trust that:
* You have the power to solve the problem - issues won't have detailed specs about HOW to build what we need, we'll leave that to you and the team.

question: When should you consider creating a custom solution instead of using community tools?
expected_output:
## Favour community tools
* Use WordPress core build tools whenever possible
* If you hit limitations, try to solve them for the wider community rather than going bespoke straight away
agent_answer:
**Short answer**

Create a custom (bespoke) solution only **after** you’ve tried the community‑maintained tools and can demonstrate that they cannot meet the requirement. In other words, go custom when:

| Situation | Why a custom solution is justified |
|-----------|------------------------------------|
| **Hard limitations in the community tool** (missing API, impossible to extend, performance bottlenecks that can’t be mitigated with caching or configuration) | The tool simply can’t do what you need, and “hacking” it would be fragile or unsustainable. |
| **Proprietary or security constraints** (e.g., the tool requires a license you can’t use, or it can’t be audited to your compliance standards) | You must own the code to satisfy internal policies. |
| **Deep integration with internal platforms** (e.g., custom logging, authentication, deployment pipelines that the community tool doesn’t support) | The integration point is so specific that a community contribution would be impractical. |
| **Business‑critical, unique functionality** that isn’t likely to be useful to the wider WordPress/open‑source community | Investing effort in a reusable internal library makes more sense than trying to “force‑fit” a generic project. |
| **When you can solve the problem for the wider community** – *but only after you’ve tried the above* – you should first open a pull‑request or file an issue. If the community accepts the change, you avoid building a bespoke solution altogether. |

**What the internal docs say**

> **Favour community tools** – *Use WordPress core build tools whenever possible. If you hit limitations, try to solve them for the wider community rather than going bespoke straight away.*  
> – *How‑we‑work / Philosophy*  

This guidance makes two points clear:

1. **Default to community tools** – they are maintained, battle‑tested, and reduce maintenance overhead for you.  
2. **Only go bespoke after a genuine limitation** – and even then, first attempt to contribute a fix upstream so the community can benefit.

**Practical workflow**

1. **Search for an existing tool** (e.g., `wp-scripts`, `@wordpress/create-block`, a popular plugin).  
2. **Evaluate** whether it meets functional, performance, security, and integration requirements.  
3. **If a limitation is found**:  
   a. Open an issue or PR in the upstream repo and see if the community can address it.  
   b. If the limitation is unlikely to be resolved (e.g., architectural mismatch, proprietary need), document the gap and obtain stakeholder approval to build a custom solution.  
4. **Document the custom solution** internally and, where appropriate, consider publishing it as an open‑source plugin so it can later become the “community tool” for future teams.

**Bottom line**

- **Start with community tools.**  
- **Switch to custom only when a real, documented limitation exists** and you’ve either tried to get it fixed upstream or have a clear business need that cannot be satisfied otherwise.  

Following this process keeps your codebase maintainable, leverages the collective effort of the open‑source ecosystem, and ensures you only invest in custom code when it truly adds value.

Document: Phpunit > `setUp` and `tearDown` (Category: guides, Source: guides_testing_phpunit.md)

### `setUp` and `tearDown` 

Before every test (method) is run, PHPUnit runs a special method called `setUp`. Likewise, after every test, it runs a method called `tearDown`. These methods can be used to set up and restore global variables, or create common objects (like users).

The WordPress testing framework includes a default `setUp` and `tearDown`. In `setUp`, the framework makes a backup copy of certain global variables (including `$wp_filter`), and starts a database transaction. This switches MySQL to using temporary tables. In `tearDown`, hooks and other globals are reset to before the test ran, the current user is reset (logged out), and the transaction is rolled back. This causes any database changes to be discarded.

These hooks mean you can do things inside your tests (like adding filters) without worrying about it affecting other tests.

You can write your own custom `setUp` and `tearDown` methods to set up state you might need to use. This could include custom globals, clearing caches, or anything we want to do on every test.

### Cache Expensive Operations
If an operation is inherently complex or slow, you can cache the result. This reduces the operation in all but the worst-case to a cache lookup, which is a constant-time operation.
This is usually a sensible solution if the result doesn't change often (for example, child post counts only change if a post is updated). If the result changes often, you may need to come up with a different solution, as the cache hit rate may not be great.

The assertion we wrote could be written a different way:
```
$this->assertSame( true, $should_be_true );
```
`assertSame` checks the value and type of the two variables matches, and is equivalent to `assertTrue( true === $should_be_true )`. While we could use either here, it's best to use the most specific assertion possible. This generates precise error messages.
Most assertions take two parameters: `$expected` and `$actual`. You should always pass the expected value first to ensure the error messages match what you'd expect.
Most assertions also take an optional last parameter `$message` which lets you specify a custom error message to be displayed next to the assertion message. You should only use this parameter when it's unclear why this assertion didn't match based on the built-in error message.
Rather than writing custom messages, name your methods descriptively. If your `test_plugin_loaded` test fails, that's enough information to debug without needing a custom message.
Congratulations, you just wrote your first PHPUnit test class! Almost every test you'll ever write follows the same pattern: run code, and check the result matches what you expect using assertions.

Document: Architecture > Value Query Limitations (Category: how-we-work, Source: how-we-work_process_architecture.md)

### Value Query Limitations
The `meta_value` field of the meta tables is not indexed, so queries against post meta values can quickly become really slow, even on small tables.
Therefore queries against meta values should be avoided on the front end. If they cannot be avoided, then the query should be cached rather aggressively.
The reliance on post meta queries is often a result of bad architectural choices. Imagine that you have an Event post type that has a start and an end date for each event. As long as this data is only used for display purposes, storing the dates in post meta is fine.
However when you need to be able to selectively display events for specific date ranges, then post meta is no longer adequate. If there are only two zones on a site that require to run this expensive query, then aggressive caching would be a solution.
However using a different storage mechanism, like the `post_date` and `post_modified` fields of the post type would be a better solution.

**Typical location**

In our React projects the standard practice is to keep JavaScript test files **next to the source files they exercise**.  
The usual pattern looks like this:

```
src/
 └─ components/
     └─ MyComponent/
         index.js               ← component code
         MyComponent.test.js    ← Jest test for that component
```

* The test file uses the `*.test.js` (or `*.spec.js`) suffix so that Jest (and tools such as create‑react‑app) can automatically discover and run it.  
* By colocating the test with the component you get a clear one‑to‑one relationship, easier navigation, and imports that are relative to the module under test.

If a team prefers a separate test tree, the internal standards also allow a top‑level `tests/` folder with a `js/` sub‑folder:

```
tests/
 └─ js/
     MyComponent.test.js
```

## Naming Things
We use the BEM naming convention as a general guide for class naming. BEM stands for Block-Element-Modifier and follows the following style of delineation to denote which level of item that we are modifying.
An element is delineated by underscores `__`, and a modifier by dashes `--`. All elements of the BEM class should be lowercased.
`.block__element--modifier { }`
This would carry out in the following example.
```
.car { /* … */ }
.car__door { /* … */ }
.car--blue { /* … */ }
```
Our **block** is a car - this represents the whole of what we're styling.
Then, we have an **element** of `__door` - this represents a single piece of the larger block that we want to style.
Finally, we have a **modifier** of `--blue` to describe a variation of the car. Perhaps our car was originally red, but we need to style this one as blue.
You can read more on BEM [here](https://href.li/?http://getbem.com/naming/).

### Nesting
Avoid nesting, and if nesting is required than absolutely nothing over 2 levels. Nesting more deeply generally indicates that the naming convention used wasn't robust enough or is not being used appropriately.
The use of BEM for class names can help avoid nesting:
```
// Avoid:
.car__door {
    .car__door--gullwing { /* … */}
}

// Prefer:
.car__door { /* … */ }
.car__door--gullwing { /* … */ }
```
The more specific modifier rule will take precedence over the element, but both rules only maintain one class' worth of specificity.
Nesting modifiers within element classes duplicates the existing meaning of the BEM class and adds unnecessary selector specificity.

### What tests should I write?
It's entirely subjective as to what sort of tests you should write, and how many tests you should write. This section is my opinion. - RM
Depending on what sort of project you want to test, the mix of tests may be different:
* For pure libraries, unit tests are typically the best way to ensure that your library behaves as expected. Libraries are expected to be self-contained units, although integration tests should be used to ensure your library interfaces with other libraries or external services correctly.
* For plugins, integration tests are mostly what you want to write. The entire purpose of most plugins is to interface with WordPress. Although writing unit tests may help here too, the effort required to mock out parts of WordPress is mostly not worth it, and you'll likely need lots of integration tests *anyway*. A lot of the benefit of testing here comes from integration tests.
* For themes or entire sites, behavioural tests will give the best value. These test that your site/theme behaves the way you expect, with links, elements, etc existing where they should on the rendered site. Unit or integration tests are not usually as important here.

question: What are some examples of industry terms that have been replaced with more inclusive language?
expected_output:
## Examples
The intention of these guidelines are to focus on the principles that you should follow, rather than providing a definitive list of terms you should avoid, however here are some real-life examples in which language used was improved to be more inclusive.
* The terms "Master/Slave" were fairly established industry terms used to describe technical operations and relationships. However there are clear issues here and in recent years, many within the industry have moved away from the use of these terms in this context in favour of more descriptive language such as "Primary/Replica". [See for example this changeset in Python](https://href.li/?https://bugs.python.org/issue34605).
* The 2011 Scrum Guide included the term "Backlog grooming" to describe a meeting in which items in the backlog are prepared for inclusion in the next sprint. Due to problematic connotations with the term ‘grooming', it was replaced with "Backlog Refinement" in the 2013 guide.
agent_answer:
Here are several concrete examples that the **Human Made “Naming Things” standards** give for industry‑wide terms that have been updated with more inclusive language:

| Original term (problematic) | Inclusive replacement | Why the change |
|-----------------------------|----------------------|----------------|
| **Master / Slave** (used to describe a primary‑secondary relationship in hardware, databases, etc.) | **Primary / Replica** (or *leader / follower*, *controller / worker*, etc.) | “Master/Slave” carries connotations of oppression and human bondage. A more descriptive, neutral pair avoids that baggage while still conveying the technical relationship. 【1†L4-L9】 |
| **Backlog grooming** (Scrum meeting to prepare backlog items) | **Backlog refinement** | “Grooming” can evoke negative or triggering connotations (e.g., animal‑grooming). The Scrum Guide switched to “refinement” to keep the meaning clear without the problematic metaphor. 【1†L10-L12】 |
| **Whitelist / Blacklist** (lists that allow or deny access) | **Safe‑list / Block‑list** (or *allow‑list / deny‑list*, *safeList / blockList* in code) | Though not racially derived, the metaphor of “white = good, black = bad” reinforces harmful color‑based stereotypes. Using explicit, descriptive terms removes that metaphor. 【4†L1-L6】 |
| **Crazy / Dumb / Cripple** (colloquial adjectives) | Alternatives such as **baffling**, **confusing**, **check for completeness and clarity** (instead of “sanity‑check”) | These words are ableist or dismissive of mental/physical conditions. Replacing them with neutral descriptors keeps communication respectful. 【4†L7-L11】 |

These examples illustrate the company’s broader guideline: **choose words that are descriptive, neutral, and free of harmful historical or cultural connotations**. The “Naming Things” document emphasizes that even widely‑used industry jargon should be examined and, when possible, updated to better reflect an inclusive culture.

* Avoid unnecessarily violent language.

question: What is the main difference between `var` and `const` in variable declaration?
agent_answer:
**Main difference**

| Aspect | `var` | `const` |
|--------|-------|---------|
| **Scope** | Function‑scoped (or global if declared outside a function). | Block‑scoped – the variable exists only within the nearest `{ … }` block. |
| **Hoisting** | Declared variables are hoisted to the top of their function and are initialized with `undefined`, so they can be accessed before the declaration (though the value will be `undefined`). | Also hoisted, but they are placed in a *temporal‑dead‑zone* and cannot be accessed until the line where they are declared; trying to do so throws a ReferenceError. |
| **Re‑assignment** | Can be re‑assigned any number of times. | May be **re‑assigned only once**; attempting to assign a new value after the initial assignment throws a TypeError. (The binding is immutable, but the value itself may be mutable – e.g., objects or arrays declared with `const` can still have their contents changed.) |
| **Redeclaration** | You can redeclare the same name within the same scope (`var x; var x;`). | Redeclaring a `const` in the same scope is a syntax error. |

In short, `var` gives you a function‑scoped, hoisted variable that can be re‑assigned and redeclared freely, whereas `const` gives you a block‑scoped variable that cannot be re‑assigned (or redeclared) after its initial definition. This is why our internal style guide recommends using `const` (or `let` when reassignment is needed) instead of `var`.

question: What is the primary concern when it comes to performance in large-scale projects?
expected_output:
# Performance
Performance is very important with the scale of the sites we work on. If it's not performant, it cannot ship. However, it's important to be pragmatic; performance is a rabbit hole that you can spend infinite time on. Shipping mostly-performant code is better than not shipping, and you can always incrementally improve it later.
Determining what is or isn't performant is tough, and this role mostly falls on the code author. However, performance should also be checked during review, especially for external plugins that may not have been created with performance in mind.
agent_answer:
In our large‑scale projects the single most important thing to watch for is **performance‑ready code**.  
The documentation states:

> *“Performance is very important with the scale of the sites we work on. If it’s not performant, it cannot ship.”*

So the primary concern is ensuring that every change is **good enough for shipping**—i.e., it meets the performance benchmarks and doesn’t introduce regressions that would prevent the product from being released. This focus on “shipping performant code” underpins all our performance‑related guidelines and code‑review checks.

question: Which WordPress functions have built-in caching capabilities?
expected_output:
At the scale of the sites we're working on, it's often useful to cache *every* post query, particularly those used in utility functions. WordPress doesn't cache these out of the box as the cache hit rate would be very low, but when we can predict that a query will happen repeatedly, we can cache it at a higher level. (Plugins are available that will handle this for you automatically, including the [Advanced Post Cache](https://href.li/?https://github.com/Automattic/advanced-post-cache) plugin which is included on VIP sites.)
Where possible, use cached functions in WordPress, as these have already handled the caching for you. This includes most high-level functions around data, including `get_post()`, `get_post_meta()`, `get_option()`, and many more. If in doubt, check the WordPress source for `wp_cache_get()` calls, or ask a friendly colleague.
agent_answer:
### Built‑in WordPress functions that **do** cache

| Function (or family) | What it caches | How it works |
|-----------------------|----------------|--------------|
| **`get_post()`** | Single post data (WP_Post object) | Uses the object cache (`wp_cache_get()`) keyed on the post ID. |
| **`get_post_meta()`** | Meta values for a post | Caches the meta array in the object cache; repeated calls for the same key return cached data. |
| **`get_option()`** | Site options (from the `options` table) | Caches option values in the object cache; the option name is the cache key. |
| **`get_term()`** and **`get_terms()`** | Taxonomy term objects and lists | These use the object cache to avoid repeated database look‑ups. |
| **`wp_get_nav_menu_items()`** | Navigation menu items | Caches the full menu tree in the object cache. |
| **`wp_get_post_terms()`** | Post‑term relationships | Uses the object cache for the relationship data. |
| **`wp_get_post_categories()`** | Category IDs for a post | Cached via the object cache. |
| **`wp_get_current_user()`** | Current user data | Stores the user object in the object cache for the duration of the request. |
| **`wp_get_theme()`** | Theme data | Caches theme information in the object cache. |
| **`wp_get_media_category()`** | Media category data | Cached in the object cache. |
| **`wp_cache_*()` family** | General object cache API | These are the primitives (`wp_cache_add()`, `wp_cache_get()`, `wp_cache_set()`, etc.) that all the above functions rely on. |

These functions are covered by the **Object Caching** layer that WordPress ships with. The cache lives in PHP memory for the request (runtime caching) and, if an object‑cache backend (Memcached, Redis, etc.) is configured, persists across requests as well.

---

#### What’s not cached

* **`get_posts()`** – intentionally not cached because the cache hit‑rate would be low and it bypasses query‑caching filters. Use `WP_Query` or cache the result yourself.  
* **`get_children()`** – also uncached; avoid unless you add your own caching layer.  

See the *Performance → Cache Queries and Requests* section in the internal standards docs for the rationale and guidance on caching custom queries.

---

#### Bottom line

If you need data that is fetched from the database, start with the high‑level functions listed above—they already have built‑in caching. For anything else, wrap the data fetch in the object‑cache API (`wp_cache_get()`/`wp_cache_set()`) or use a caching plugin that follows the same pattern.
