## Runtime Caching
Runtime caching is similar to object caching, but is only stored for a single request. Objects are stored in PHP's memory until the end of the request and are not persisted across requests. (Runtime caching is sometimes called "local" caching.)
The simplest form of runtime caching in PHP is global or static variables. For example, the `$wp_query` and `$post` global variables are runtime caches. Runtime caching is stored entirely in PHP's memory, so it does not incur the latency overhead of hitting an external object cache server.
In WordPress, a runtime cache is built into the object cache layer, which typically ensures good performance for repeated cache lookups, while still using a persistent object cache across all servers. You can also [specifically mark a cache group as non-persistent](https://href.li/?https://developer.wordpress.org/reference/functions/wp_cache_add_non_persistent_groups/), which will turn it into a runtime-only cache.

---

Document: Caching > Fragment Caching (Category: standards, Source: standards_backend_caching.md)

### Fragment Caching
Fragment caching is a technique which combines page caching and object caching. Rather than caching a full HTML page, fragment caching stores smaller HTML strings ("fragments") in the object cache. This allows sharing generated HTML between pages and potentially between users.
For example, you might want to fragment-cache a single template part, such as the sidebar or header.
This technique may be useful if the HTML generation itself is expensive, or if caching all the underlying functions used by the template is tricky. It provides an easy-to-implement way to cache, but the downside is that the cached fragment can't be reused for slightly different output or in other contexts (such as a REST API). Typically, it's better to use the object cache on the underlying functions instead.

---

[5] chunk_id: standards_backend_caching_chunk_8 | document_id: standards_backend_caching
Document: Caching > Object Caching (Category: standards, Source: standards_backend_caching.md)

Similarly to page caching, WordPress provides a drop-in for object caching at `wp-content/object-cache.php`. We typically a [Memcache](https://href.li/?https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memcached) backend server with the [memcached drop-in](https://href.li/?https://github.com/humanmade/wordpress-pecl-memcached-object-cache). However, this is an implementation detail, and you typically won't need to worry about this.
"Memcache" and "Memcached" are interchangeable names for the backend cache server. However, the name of the PHP extension used on the app server is [Memcached](https://href.li/?http://php.net/manual/en/book.memcached.php), which is not the same as the [legacy Memcache extension](https://href.li/?http://php.net/manual/en/book.memcached.php).
Interacting with the object cache is typically done through the [WordPress object cache API](https://href.li/?https://codex.wordpress.org/Class_Reference/WP_Object_Cache). The `wp_cache_*()` family of functions should be always used instead of accessing the underlying memcache implementation.

question: What should be included in the main plugin.php file?
expected_output:
### `plugin.php`
Your main `plugin.php` file should include the [plugin header comment](https://href.li/?https://developer.wordpress.org/plugins/the-basics/header-requirements/) and any plugin constants (such as `const FILE = __FILE__` for easiest use of `plugins_url()` and related functions). It should load in any namespace files, register any autoloaders, and handle the initial hooking into WordPress.
**This file should be the only file to contain [side-effects](/standards/style/php/#file-layout) (function calls outside a function).**
For complex plugins, you may want to move the actual `add_action`/`add_filter` calls into a main function in the namespace, and simply call that function from `plugin.php`. (This function is typically named `bootstrap()` or `setup()` to indicate it is responsible for setting up the plugin's behaviour.)
For super-simple plugins with only a handful of functions, you can declare functions in this file as well. This should be done sparingly, as you'll need to ignore the coding standards checks on the file; if in doubt, split the functions out.
agent_answer:
**What goes into the main `plugin.php` file?** | Item | Why it’s needed | Example snippet | |------|-----------------|-----------------| | **Plugin header comment** | WordPress reads this to display the plugin on the Plugins page and to validate the plugin. It must contain at least `Plugin Name`, and may include `Description`, `Version`, `Author`, etc. | ```php
/**
* Plugin Name: My Custom Plugin
* Description: Adds X, Y, Z functionality.
* Version: 1.0.0
* Author: Company Name
* Text Domain: my-plugin
*/
``` | | **Core constants** | Handy for generating URLs or file paths (`plugins_url()`, `plugin_dir_path()` etc.). Using a constant for the main file makes future refactors easier. | ```php
const MY_PLUGIN_FILE = __FILE__;
``` | | **Autoloader registration** | Loads your plugin’s classes/ functions when they’re first used. For a typical HM‑style plugin you’ll use the `HM\Autoloader` or the WordPress `spl_autoload_register`. | ```php
require_once __DIR__ . '/inc/autoloader.php';
``` | | **Namespace/require files** | If your plugin splits code into sub‑namespaces (e.g., `HM\Plugin\FeatureA`) you’ll include the bootstrap file(s) or register the PSR‑4 map here. | ```php
require_once __DIR__ . '/inc/feature-a.php';
``` | | **Initial hook setup** | Register all the `add_action()`/`add_filter()` calls that bootstrap the plugin’s behaviour. In many cases you’ll wrap these calls in a *bootstrap* or *setup* function, and then call that function from `plugin.php` (so that the file itself has no side‑effects except the very first `add_action()` calls). | ```php
function my_plugin_setup() {\n add_action( 'init', __NAMESPACE__ . '\\init' );\n // …other hooks\n}\nadd_action( 'plugins_loaded', __NAMESPACE__ . '\\my_plugin_setup' );\n``` | | **Side‑effect‑free design** | The file should be the *only* file that contains side‑effects (direct calls to functions or class constructors). All other code should live in included files or within functions that are only called via hooks. | – (No other code here except the bootstrap hooks) | ### TL;DR 1. **Header comment** – WordPress metadata. 2. **Constants** – e.g., `const FILE = __FILE__`. 3. **Autoloader & namespace files** – load your plugin’s internal code. 4. **Bootstrap function** – register all hooks (`add_action`, `add_filter`). 5. **One single side‑effect** – the bootstrap call that WordPress executes (usually via `plugins_loaded`). Follow the layout in the `standards_structure.md` section “`plugin.php`” – that file is the canonical reference for what the main plugin file must contain.

question: What alternative methods can be used to track page views?
expected_output:
## Avoid Writes on Page Views
You should avoid writing to the database on page views. Writing anything simply when a page is loaded is a surefire way to kill the database. This applies on any page view, including regular frontend pages and dashboard pages. You should only write to the database after a form submission (or Ajax `PUT` or `POST` request). (Note that this also applies to the filesystem, but you shouldn't write to the filesystem anyway.)
Writes to the database can cause row or table locking, in addition to invalidating the various caches throughout WordPress and the database. Additionally, it means that pages cannot be cached properly.
If you need to track page views or similar, consider a dedicated service, including external services like Google Analytics. You're often better off using these and pulling data back to the site via their API. (This is how [hm-top-posts](https://href.li/?https://github.com/humanmade/hm-top-posts) works, for example.) WordPress is built for a read-heavy workload, whereas analytics are a write-heavy workload, so a dedicated service built for analytics is usually a better option.
agent_answer:
**Alternative ways to track page views (according to our internal documentation)**  

| Alternative | How it works | Why it’s preferred |
|-------------|--------------|--------------------|
| **Dedicated analytics services (e.g., Google Analytics, Mixpanel, Amplitude)** | Add a small script tag or SDK that reports each page view to the service. The service stores the data in a write‑heavy, highly‑optimized backend and exposes APIs for retrieval. | Keeps the WordPress database free from heavy write traffic, avoids locking and cache invalidation, and lets you leverage powerful analytics features (segmentation, funnels, real‑time dashboards). |
| **External analytics API integration** | Pull aggregated view counts or events from the external service via its REST/GraphQL API and display or use them on the site. | Allows you to keep your own UI/UX while still benefiting from a scalable analytics infrastructure. |
| **Server‑side proxy or micro‑service** | Send page‑view data from the front‑end to a lightweight micro‑service that writes to a fast, write‑optimized store (e.g., Redis, ClickHouse). | Gives more control over data schema and privacy while still decoupling heavy writes from the main WordPress database. |
| **Log‑based analysis** | Let the web server (e.g., Nginx/Apache) write access logs and run batch jobs to parse page‑view counts. | Eliminates real‑time write pressure on the database and can be used for archival or long‑term analytics. |

> **Key point from our standards:**  
> *“If you need to track page views or similar, consider a dedicated service, including external services like Google Analytics. You're often better off using these and pulling data back to the site via their API.”* (Standards → Backend Performance)

So, rather than inserting a row for every page view, you should off‑load the write‑heavy workload to an analytics platform or a separate service and then fetch aggregated data as needed.

question: How can web fonts be loaded efficiently to improve perceived performance?
expected_output:
## Perceived Performance
Perceived performance is how performant the user perceives the site, as opposed to the technical measurements of performance. While technical performance is important, perceived performance can have a greater effect on the users willingness to stay on the site.
Perceived performance is typically measured as the time it takes for the content to be usable, this may occur before assets have finished rendering (images, fonts, JavaScript).
Perceived performance can be improved by
* Using system fonts
* If web fonts are used, initial render ought to use system fonts and switch to the web font once it completes loading (FOUT). In recent browsers this can be achieved in CSS using [`font-display: swap`](https://href.li/?https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@font-face/font-display) in older browsers the [Font Face Observer](https://href.li/?https://fontfaceobserver.com/) JavaScript library can be used.
* Avoid unnecessary jumps.
* As assets load, images, advertisements, video and other embeds, they can cause text content to jump around on the page. Avoid this by using CSS and/or width and height attributes to allow space for this content to fill.
agent_answer:
### Key Strategies for Efficient Web‑Font Loading (Perceived‑Performance Focus) | Goal | What to Do | Why It Helps | |------|------------|--------------| | **Keep the first paint fast** | 1. **Use a system‑font stack as the default**
2. **Load the web font asynchronously** | The user sees text immediately, avoiding a blank or “flash‑of‑unrendered‑text” (FOIT). | | **Avoid layout jumps** | 1. **Specify font‑face `font-display: swap`** (or use a JS polyfill for old browsers)
2. **Set `font-weight`/`font-style` on the ``** | Text shows in a fallback until the web font is ready, then swaps in without re‑flow. | | **Reduce network cost** | 1. **Subset fonts** – only include characters you actually need.
2. **Compress font files (woff2)**.
3. **Use HTTP/2 push or `rel="preload"`** to prime the connection. | Fewer bytes → faster download → quicker swap. | | **Prevent FOIT/flash‑of‑styled‑text** | 1. **Avoid `font-display: optional`** (it may hide the text entirely).
2. **Use a small, lightweight fallback family** (e.g., system‑sans serif). | Ensures the text is always legible and visible. | --- #### Practical Implementation Steps 1. **Define a reliable fallback stack** ```css body { font-family: system-ui, -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", Roboto, sans-serif; } ``` *The browser will render text with a system font right away.* 2. **Declare the web font with `font-display: swap`** ```css @font-face { font-family: "MyBrand"; src: url("/fonts/MyBrand.woff2") format("woff2"); font-display: swap; /* <-- swap in when loaded */ } ``` - **Older browsers**: Wrap the CSS in a conditional or use the [Font‑Face‑Observer](https://fontfaceobserver.com/) library to trigger a class change once the font is ready. 3. **Preload the most critical font file** ```html ``` - This hints the browser to start fetching early, especially on HTTP/2 where the header can be sent first. 4. **Subset and compress** - Use tools like [glyphhanger](https://github.com/filamentgroup/glyphhanger) or [Font Subsetter](https://github.com/fonttools/fonttools) to include only the glyphs you actually use. - Serve the resulting `.woff2` (or `.woff` if you need fallback support) which is ~2× smaller than uncompressed OTF/TTF. 5. **Avoid “flash‑of‑unstyled‑text” (FOIT)** - `font-display: block` will block rendering until the font is loaded – not recommended. - `font-display: swap` is the safe default; it guarantees visible text. --- #### Example ```html ``` When the page loads: 1. Browser immediately renders text with the system font. 2. It starts downloading the `Roboto` font (preload speeds this). 3. Once downloaded, the font swaps in without re‑layout, keeping the perceived load time low. --- ### Bottom Line - **Always render text first with a system fallback.** - **Load web fonts asynchronously** and let the browser swap them in when ready (`font-display: swap`). - **Preload, subset, and compress** the font files to shrink payload. - **Avoid FOIT** by not using `font-display: block` or `optional`. By following these steps, you ensure that users see content immediately and experience a smoother, faster‑seeming page load.

The main usage of [`sanitize_text_field()`](https://href.li/?https://developer.wordpress.org/reference/functions/sanitize_text_field/) function is to sanitise the data provided by text input fields in forms. But it's useful for sanitising any kind of data that you want to be plain text.

### Using Libraries
At the scale of projects Human Made typically takes on, rolling your own is more time-effective and less frustrating than using libraries for styling. However, there are certain situation where a library can be useful and used wholesale.

(Information drawn from the company’s internal standards documentation)

| # | Drawback | Why it matters | What the docs say |
|---|----------|----------------|-------------------|
| 1 | **Code bloat / unused orphan code** | A large library often contains many components that a project never uses. Those unused parts still ship with the bundle, increasing file size, load time, and memory usage. | “A large frameworks or library such as Bootstrap or Font Awesome is unlikely to be the right solution… You will likely only use a tiny portion of the entire library, leaving the rest as unused orphan code that provides no benefit and adds to the complexity of the codebase.” (Standards > Using Libraries) |

| 3 | **Performance impact** | Bigger bundles mean longer download times, more JavaScript to parse, and potentially slower runtime performance, which hurts the user experience on mobile and low‑bandwidth connections. | The standards emphasis on keeping CSS minimal for mobile‑first performance (Standards > Responsive Styles) implies that larger libraries would conflict with that goal. |
| 4 | **Learning curve & onboarding** | Large frameworks introduce many conventions, patterns, and a steep learning curve. Document: Testing > What tests should I write? (Category: guides, Source: guides_testing.md)

Each project will have its own requirements for the numer and type of tests you need. Large site builds may have unit and integration tests for underlying plugins and libraries, and behavioural tests for the theme as a whole.
Typically, libraries and plugins should aim for 100% test coverage, whether unit or integration tests. The specific nature of these tests depends on the plugin at hand. On the other hand, themes and sites warrant much less testing, as they're immediately user-facing, and are less likely to break in subtle ways.
It's important to always be mindful of how much time and effort testing takes, and to be pragmatic. It'd be great to have the entire codebase of every site 100% unit tested, but that's often not realistic. Instead, test the underlying custom behaviour (plugins), and use behavioural tests to test edge-case functionality. Redistributable projects (open source plugins and libraries, e.g.) should be generally held to a higher standard, as they're much more likely to hit edge cases.

The assertion we wrote could be written a different way:

`assertSame` checks the value and type of the two variables matches, and is equivalent to `assertTrue( true === $should_be_true )`. While we could use either here, it's best to use the most specific assertion possible. This generates precise error messages.

### Quotes within the `url` function
The `url()` function within CSS accepts parameters with both quotes and without quotes in the v3 spec. However, quoteless parameters require more escaping and special care; using quotes avoids having to remember special escaping rules and makes the values work more reliably.
```
// Avoid:
div {

}

div {
    background-image: url( "../my-background.jpg" );
}

## Progressive Enhancement
Progressive enhancement emphasizes core webpage content first. This strategy then progressively adds more nuanced and technically rigorous layers of presentation and features on top of the content as the end-user's browser/internet connection allow.\*
The order of displaying content:
First content (HTML), then presentation (CSS) and after that client-side scripting ([Chocolatey Layers of Progressive Enhancement](https://href.li/?https://alistapart.com/article/understandingprogressiveenhancement)).
The basic render should include content for the lowest end browsers and allow for JavaScript to fail. Additional content (carousel frames, items behind accordions, etc) can be loaded and rendered via JavaScript.
React projects should include server side rendering, this can take one of two approaches:
* JavaScript first: basic WordPress PHP templates can be used to render the initial response and be replaced/improved upon with React.

question: Why is it difficult to debug unbounded queries?
expected_output:
## Unbounded Queries
It's super easy to kill a large site by forgetting to put a limit on your query. Queries should always have an upper bound to ensure you don't try and load 400,000 posts into memory. This can be tough to spot locally with only a few test posts, so it's important to be careful about checking every query.
When writing database queries or post queries, always include an upper limit. If you need to get every item, reconsider the need to do so first, and whether you can change the process altogether. Unbounded queries are fine when you're only working with a few items in the database, but present problems as the site scales. (They can be difficult to debug as well, as the site may just go down for no reason in the middle of the night; just ask Ryan about downtime during the retreat.)
If you can do so, rethink the way you're storing or presenting data in the first place. You may be able to present pagination to the user instead, or use an infinite scroll technique to load items in batches instead.
agent_answer:
Unbounded queries (i.e., queries that pull *all* rows from a table without a `LIMIT` clause or an equivalent pagination strategy) are notoriously hard to debug for a few reasons:

| Why they’re hard to debug | What happens |
|---------------------------|--------------|
| **They only show up at scale** | In a local dev environment you may have a handful of posts, so `WP_Query(... 'posts_per_page' => -1)` or a raw `SELECT * FROM wp_posts` will finish quickly. On production, that same query can try to fetch hundreds of thousands of rows, consuming all available memory or network bandwidth. The symptom is often a sudden site‑wide crash or a “timeout” that appears out of nowhere. |
| **Symptoms are non‑specific** | A server that “just goes down” in the middle of the night can be caused by many things: a cron job, a memory leak, a slow external API, etc. Unbounded queries add a *hidden* load that only manifests under heavy traffic, making it difficult to trace back to the offending code. |
| **Local testing is misleading** | With only a few test posts, the query looks fine. The docs warn: *“It can be tough to spot locally with only a few test posts, so it’s important to be careful about checking every query.”* A test environment that never reaches the production volume will never reproduce the failure. |
| **No clear breakpoint** | Because the query can start to overload the system at any time (e.g., after a traffic spike), there’s no obvious point to place a debugger or log statement that will catch the problem. |
| **Impact on the whole stack** | The query may exhaust MySQL’s buffers, exhaust PHP’s memory, or saturate the network, affecting other unrelated processes and services. This makes it hard to isolate the root cause without a full‑stack view. |

In short, **unbounded queries can silently consume resources at scale, and their failure mode (resource exhaustion, timeouts, crashes) is generic enough that it’s hard to point it back to the original query without careful logging, pagination, or moving the heavy work to a background job**. The internal guidelines therefore strongly advise always setting an upper bound (e.g., `posts_per_page` > 0 or a `LIMIT` clause) and, if you truly need to process everything, to do it in an offline, batched process like a WP‑CLI command or cron job.

Document: Performance > Unbounded Queries (Category: standards, Source: standards_backend_performance.md)

The typical unbounded query in WordPress is using `WP_Query` with `'posts_per_page' => -1`. **Do not do this.** Likewise, raw database queries without a `LIMIT` clause should not be used.
If you really do need to touch every post in the database, consider whether you can move your code into an offline solution; that is, into a wp-cli command or a cron task. This ensures that end users are shielded from potential scaling issues, and makes the operation fail-safe.
Here is an example of querying all posts with bounded queries:
```
 'post',
    'post_status' => 'publish',
    'posts_per_page' => 100,
    'paged' => 1,
    'orderby' => 'ID', 
];

do {
    $query = new WP_Query( $args );
    foreach ( $query->posts as $post ) {
        the_ID();
    }
    $args['paged']++;
} while ( $args['paged'] max_num_pages );
```
While this will still retrieve every item from the database, paginating through results reduces load on MySQL as well as data passed over the wire. This should still generally be avoided or offloaded where possible.

[5] chunk_id: standards_backend_caching_chunk_13 | document_id: standards_backend_caching
Document: Caching > Query Caching (Category: standards, Source: standards_backend_caching.md)

## Query Caching
Query caching is the lowest level of caching, and takes place entirely within the database. MySQL [maintains a cache](https://href.li/?https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/5.6/en/query-cache.html) of `SELECT` queries with their results, which allows any queries which aren't cached at a higher level to still be cached.
Query caching is very basic. It caches the result against the exact bytes of the `SELECT` query, so queries that differ even slightly (such as `SELECT` vs `select`) will be stored under separate cache keys. It is unable to cache any queries that contain dynamic functions (such as `RAND()` or `NOW()`). Additionally, it is cleared on every update to the table (including `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE`). The query cache cannot be partially invalidated and is controlled at the hosting infrastructure level.
Due to these limitations, the query cache should be regarded as a cache-of-last-resort. It is not a substitute for well-written custom caching code in the object cache, and should not be relied upon. Generally, you should write code as if the query cache does not exist.

*From our internal “How‑We‑Work” philosophy guide:*

3. **Keep a living catalog** – an internal page or wiki that shows available plugins, their purpose, and links to their repositories or installation instructions.

Doing these steps ensures that any plugin we add plugs into the ecosystem cleanly, is easy to maintain, and can coexist with other plugins without clashes.

## What's the alternative?
We can't possibly write code to handle every potential use case, so instead we should encourage a large ecosystem around our plugins. To enable plugins to work coherently, we need to make sure they're as extensible as WordPress core itself. In addition, we should have a resources page that lists other available plugins, and promotes them as much as possible.

# Third Party Plugin Reviews
Human Made regularly makes use of existing third party plugins for WordPress during project delivery, subject to our company-wide standards for performance, security, and accessibility.
In the past the company has maintained a list of pre-approved third-party plugins for use on Altis and WordPress VIP, but due to differing and changing requirements between clients this is no longer the case. Delivery teams are responsible for ensuring that third-party plugins are fit for purpose for each project, and that they meet our engineering standards.
Within the WordPress ecosystem there are a number of long-established and trusted vendors who publish high quality plugins that we frequently use and recommend between projects. By default the delivery team should prefer using solutions from Altis Cloud Partners and WordPress VIP Agency Partners as they typically operate at the highest engineering standards.

---

[4] chunk_id: standards_structure_chunk_8 | document_id: standards_structure
Document: Structure > `plugin.php` (Category: standards, Source: standards_structure.md)

### `plugin.php`
Your main `plugin.php` file should include the [plugin header comment](https://href.li/?https://developer.wordpress.org/plugins/the-basics/header-requirements/) and any plugin constants (such as `const FILE = __FILE__` for easiest use of `plugins_url()` and related functions). It should load in any namespace files, register any autoloaders, and handle the initial hooking into WordPress.
**This file should be the only file to contain [side-effects](/standards/style/php/#file-layout) (function calls outside a function).**
For complex plugins, you may want to move the actual `add_action`/`add_filter` calls into a main function in the namespace, and simply call that function from `plugin.php`. (This function is typically named `bootstrap()` or `setup()` to indicate it is responsible for setting up the plugin's behaviour.)
For super-simple plugins with only a handful of functions, you can declare functions in this file as well. This should be done sparingly, as you'll need to ignore the coding standards checks on the file; if in doubt, split the functions out.

---

[5] chunk_id: guides_testing_chunk_5 | document_id: guides_testing
Document: Testing > What tests should I write? (Category: guides, Source: guides_testing.md)

Each project will have its own requirements for the numer and type of tests you need. Large site builds may have unit and integration tests for underlying plugins and libraries, and behavioural tests for the theme as a whole.
Typically, libraries and plugins should aim for 100% test coverage, whether unit or integration tests. The specific nature of these tests depends on the plugin at hand. On the other hand, themes and sites warrant much less testing, as they're immediately user-facing, and are less likely to break in subtle ways.
It's important to always be mindful of how much time and effort testing takes, and to be pragmatic. It'd be great to have the entire codebase of every site 100% unit tested, but that's often not realistic. Instead, test the underlying custom behaviour (plugins), and use behavioural tests to test edge-case functionality. Redistributable projects (open source plugins and libraries, e.g.) should be generally held to a higher standard, as they're much more likely to hit edge cases.

question: How can overusing Sass functionality negatively impact a codebase?
expected_output:
## Writing Sass
Sass can be an incredibly powerful tool on large projects. Things like variables, partials, and mixins help us write more maintainable CSS. However it is important to remember 2 things.
* Be aware of the CSS that is created by the SASS you write.
* Just because SASS has lots of cool functionality, be wary of overusing it! Otherwise you may end up with a codebase that is difficult to maintain and hard for other developers to get their heads around!
agent_answer:
### How over‑using Sass can hurt a codebase

The company’s internal style‑guides (see *Css > Writing Sass*) warn that “just because SASS has lots of cool functionality, be wary of overusing it! Otherwise you may end up with a codebase that is difficult to maintain and hard for other developers to get their heads around.”

In practice this means that leaning too heavily on Sass’s advanced features can lead to several problems:

| Issue | Why it happens | What to watch out for |
|-------|----------------|-----------------------|
| **Huge, hard‑to‑read generated CSS** | Mixins that output many selectors, deep nesting, and recursive functions can create a large CSS bundle that is difficult to understand at a glance. | Keep an eye on the final CSS size; run `sass --style=expanded` and compare with the output of plain CSS. |
| **Unexpected side effects** | Variables, mixins, and functions can be called from many places. Changing a variable value can ripple through the entire stylesheet, causing subtle bugs. | Document where a variable is altered and prefer local (scoped) variables when possible. |
| **Over‑specific selectors** | Heavy nesting or mixins that append selector modifiers can produce selectors that are too specific, making overrides difficult. | Use the BEM naming convention and avoid nesting beyond 3–4 levels. |
| **Hard to refactor** | When business logic is tucked inside mixins, refactoring a UI component may require hunting through many Sass files. | Keep mixins small, single‑purpose, and well‑named; document the public API of each mixin. |
| **Performance hit** | A gigantic compiled CSS file slows load times and can strain the browser’s rendering engine. | Regularly run a CSS bundle‑size audit (`sass --watch` → `gzip` size). |
| **Poor collaboration** | New developers or designers may struggle to understand the “magic” happening inside a mixin or function. | Add clear comments and example usage for each mixin or function. |

#### Example: variable misuse

> **Avoid**  
> ```scss
> :root {
>     --hm-red: #D24632; /* Better as a Sass variable */
> }
> ```  
> (From *Css > Variable Usage*)

> **Prefer**  
> ```scss
> .car {
>     --transparent: rgba( 0, 0, 0, 0 );
>     --solid: rgba( 0, 0, 0, 1 );
>     background-image: linear-gradient( var(--solid), var(--transparent) );
> }
> ```

When a global CSS variable is defined once and reused everywhere, a later change can unintentionally affect many components. Using a Sass variable keeps the value in a single place and prevents cascade surprises.

#### Bottom line

*Use Sass for the things it solves best—variables, partials, and small, reusable mixins.*  
*Avoid treating Sass as a full‑blown “programming language” that hides too much logic from the generated CSS.*  

Sticking to the style‑guides’ recommendations will keep the stylesheet maintainable, readable, and easier for the team to collaborate on.

question: When is caching not a suitable solution for expensive operations?
expected_output:
### Cache Expensive Operations
If an operation is inherently complex or slow, you can cache the result. This reduces the operation in all but the worst-case to a cache lookup, which is a constant-time operation.
This is usually a sensible solution if the result doesn't change often (for example, child post counts only change if a post is updated). If the result changes often, you may need to come up with a different solution, as the cache hit rate may not be great.
agent_answer:
**When caching is *not* the right tool for an expensive operation** | Situation | Why caching may be unsuitable | Suggested alternative(s) | |-----------|------------------------------|--------------------------| | **The result changes very frequently** (e.g., updates on every request, per‑user data that is mutated in real time) | The cache hit rate drops dramatically; the cache can become a source of stale data or a bottleneck that still requires a write operation for every change. | • Re‑architect to store the data in a more appropriate place (e.g., use a relational column instead of post‑meta for time‑based queries).
• Use a write‑through or write‑behind cache that invalidates/updates more aggressively.
• Perform the expensive logic on demand without caching if the number of calls is low. | | **The operation is inherently small or cheap** (e.g., a quick lookup or a calculation that completes in a few milliseconds) | Adding cache storage (memory lookup, serialization, network hop) can actually slow the overall flow because the overhead of cache management outweighs the savings from avoiding the calculation. | Keep the operation inline; or use an in‑memory, lightweight runtime cache if you want to avoid repeated work within a single request. | | **The data is highly contextual or unique to each request** (e.g., user‑specific, session‑specific, or depends on request‑level state) | A global cache key would mix data from different contexts, leading to data leakage or incorrect results. | Cache at a more granular scope (e.g., per user or per session) or avoid caching entirely and rely on efficient computation or pre‑computed aggregates stored in a database. | | **The operation requires a very high cache consistency guarantee** (e.g., financial transactions, inventory levels) | A stale value can cause business logic errors; if the cost of a cache miss is too high, it is safer to always recompute. | Use a strongly consistent store (e.g., transactional database) or a queue that recomputes values asynchronously while still returning a stale value if acceptable. | | **The cache hit rate is low due to a small set of distinct inputs** | With a low hit rate the cache adds complexity without much benefit; you’ll still hit the expensive logic often. | Use a simple memoization inside the request, or redesign the operation to be cheaper (e.g., pre‑aggregate data). | | **The operation’s result is largely the same across many requests but the operation itself is a *side effect* (e.g., writes to a log, sends a notification)** | Caching would skip the side‑effect, changing the system’s behavior. | Do not cache; ensure the side‑effect happens each time, or off‑load the side‑effect to a background job that runs on demand. | ### Key takeaway from our internal *Performance* standards > *"If an operation is inherently complex or slow, you can cache the result. This reduces the operation in all but the worst‑case to a cache lookup, which is a constant‑time operation. This is usually a sensible solution if the result doesn’t change often. If the result changes often, you may need to come up with a different solution, as the cache hit rate may not be great."* – **Standards > Cache Expensive Operations** So, caching is a great tool when the operation is **expensive** *and* its results are **stable**. When either of those conditions fails—frequent changes, small cost, unique per‑request data, strict consistency, or a low hit rate—the cache is more trouble than it’s worth. In those cases, consider redesigning the data model, using a different storage mechanism, or computing the value on demand.

Document: Caching > Fragment Caching (Category: standards, Source: standards_backend_caching.md)

### Fragment Caching
Fragment caching is a technique which combines page caching and object caching. Rather than caching a full HTML page, fragment caching stores smaller HTML strings ("fragments") in the object cache. This allows sharing generated HTML between pages and potentially between users.
For example, you might want to fragment-cache a single template part, such as the sidebar or header.
This technique may be useful if the HTML generation itself is expensive, or if caching all the underlying functions used by the template is tricky. It provides an easy-to-implement way to cache, but the downside is that the cached fragment can't be reused for slightly different output or in other contexts (such as a REST API). Typically, it's better to use the object cache on the underlying functions instead.

---

# Caching
Caching happens at many layers during a typical request, from the user's computer all the way through to the database behind WordPress. Controlling these caches is important to ensure a performant site.

[4] chunk_id: standards_backend_caching_chunk_11 | document_id: standards_backend_caching
Document: Caching > Runtime Caching (Category: standards, Source: standards_backend_caching.md)

## Runtime Caching
Runtime caching is similar to object caching, but is only stored for a single request. Objects are stored in PHP's memory until the end of the request and are not persisted across requests. (Runtime caching is sometimes called "local" caching.)
The simplest form of runtime caching in PHP is global or static variables. For example, the `$wp_query` and `$post` global variables are runtime caches. Runtime caching is stored entirely in PHP's memory, so it does not incur the latency overhead of hitting an external object cache server.
In WordPress, a runtime cache is built into the object cache layer, which typically ensures good performance for repeated cache lookups, while still using a persistent object cache across all servers. You can also [specifically mark a cache group as non-persistent](https://href.li/?https://developer.wordpress.org/reference/functions/wp_cache_add_non_persistent_groups/), which will turn it into a runtime-only cache.

---

[5] chunk_id: how-we-work_process_architecture_chunk_29 | document_id: how-we-work_process_architecture
Document: Architecture > Value Query Limitations (Category: how-we-work, Source: how-we-work_process_architecture.md)

### Value Query Limitations
The `meta_value` field of the meta tables is not indexed, so queries against post meta values can quickly become really slow, even on small tables.
Therefore queries against meta values should be avoided on the front end. If they cannot be avoided, then the query should be cached rather aggressively.
The reliance on post meta queries is often a result of bad architectural choices. Imagine that you have an Event post type that has a start and an end date for each event. As long as this data is only used for display purposes, storing the dates in post meta is fine.
However when you need to be able to selectively display events for specific date ranges, then post meta is no longer adequate. If there are only two zones on a site that require to run this expensive query, then aggressive caching would be a solution.
However using a different storage mechanism, like the `post_date` and `post_modified` fields of the post type would be a better solution.

question: What are the specific formatting rules for CSS declarations in the preferred code style?
agent_answer:
**CSS declaration formatting (per our internal style guide)**  

| Rule | What it looks like | Why it matters |
|------|--------------------|----------------|
| **Each selector on its own line** |```css\n.foo,\n.baz,\n.bar {\n…\n}\n```| Keeps the selector list readable and makes it easy to spot missing commas or stray selectors. |
| **Space before the opening brace** |```css\n.foo { … }\n```| Consistent with the WordPress CSS coding standards we inherit and keeps the code visually tidy. |
| **Trailing brace on its own line** |```css\n.foo {\n…\n}\n```| Helps the diff engine spot changes and makes the block’s boundaries clear. |
| **Each declaration on its own line** |```css\n.foo {\n    color: #000;\n    background-color: linear-gradient( to bottom, #fff, #ccc );\n}\n```| Improves readability, makes it easier to comment out a single rule, and aids tools that count lines of code. |
| **Semicolon after every declaration (even the last one)** |```css\n.foo {\n    color: #000;\n    background-color: linear-gradient( to bottom, #fff, #ccc );\n}\n```| Avoids silent syntax errors when new declarations are appended and matches the WordPress coding style. |
| **Blank line between selector sets** |```css\n.foo { … }\n\n.bar { … }\n```| Keeps logical blocks visually separated and prevents accidental merging of unrelated rules. |
| **Double‑quoted values where strings are used** |```css\nfont-family: "Helvetica Neue", sans-serif;\n```| Consistent with WordPress’s preference and avoids issues with characters that could be mis‑interpreted (e.g., spaces, commas). |
| **Spaces inside parentheses** |```css\nlinear-gradient( to bottom, #fff, #ccc );\n```| Improves legibility of functions and aligns with the style we adopt from WordPress. |
| **Use of `rem` for lengths when appropriate** |```css\nfont-size: 1rem;\n```| Encourages scalable, accessible design (although the “basic styles” example uses it; it’s not a hard‑coded rule, just a recommended practice). |

> **Bottom line:**  
> 1. Start each selector on its own line, put a space before `{` and a newline after `}`.  
> 2. Put each property/value pair on a separate line, end each with a semicolon.  
> 3. Quote string values, add a blank line between rule‑blocks, and keep spacing inside functions.  

These rules are taken directly from the **`standards_style_css.md`** internal documentation (see the “Basic Styles” section). If you need a concrete example, the doc shows:

```css
.foo,
.baz,
.bar {
    color: #000;
    background-color: linear-gradient( to bottom, #fff, #ccc );
    font-size: 1rem;
    font-family: "Helvetica Neue", sans-serif;
}

.foo-bar { /* … */ }
```

Follow the same pattern for all CSS in the codebase.

# Performance
Performance is something that needs to be considered early in the architecture and design of features, rather than corrected for at the end. When we talk about performance at this level, we're talking about the *performance characteristics* of the process or algorithm (this is also called the *characteristic performance*).
When discussing performance characteristics, it's common to talk about "algorithms". This doesn't mean a formal mathematical process, but rather discussing the abstract process rather than the specific steps. For example, the algorithm for calculating the number of posts for an author could be:
* Set the counter to zero
* Fetch all posts
* For every post:
+ If the post is not by the author, skip it
+ Add one to the counter
It might be helpful to think of an algorithm as a single function.

---

Document: Architecture > Job Scheduling System (Category: how-we-work, Source: how-we-work_process_architecture.md)

### Job Scheduling System
An asynchronous job handler is a requirement for every application. The least reliable solution is WP Cron, so often Linux crons can be used. Certain hosts offer a separate job infrastructure that is independent of web requests, which is the ideal scenario.

### Key Query Limitations
An object can have multiple meta entries with the same key associated to it. This can lead to difficult to detect bugs, if the meta API functions are used wrong:
* `add_*_meta()` accepts a `$unique` argument. If set to `false` (the default), a new entry with the same key will be added. If set to `true`, nothing will be saved.

Document: Architecture > Client Side Integrations (Category: how-we-work, Source: how-we-work_process_architecture.md)

### Client Side Integrations
The first type are integrations are client side only. This means that they impact the front end, without any impact on the infrastructure. A common example would be Google Analytics, or integrating a third party commenting system.
As the application does not have direct access to these external services, there are limitations on how the PHP layer and often also the front end can interact with them. As an example if related articles are being pulled in from an external service using a JavaScript snippet injecting content directly into the DOM, then there's no way to implement a fallback on the PHP layer if the external service does not respond.
Integrations that are client side only do not impact the PHP-generated page delivery performance of the application. However if the rendering of the front end is impacted, then this needs to be taken into account. A placeholder or a loading indicator could be displayed while the interaction with the external services is being done.

question: What are some potential issues with using static variables?
expected_output: You may want to avoid `static` variables (which are not the same as static class properties), which are stored only in the context of the specific function. These can become tough to invalidate or otherwise manage during testing.
agent_answer:
**Static variables (e.g., `static $foo = …;` inside a function or a static class property) can be convenient, but they introduce several problems that the company’s best‑practice guides warn about.  Below are the main issues that have been documented in our internal standards and coding guidelines:**

| Issue | Why it matters | Reference |
|-------|----------------|-----------|
| **Hidden global state** | A static variable lives in a single place that persists across the life‑time of the request.  It behaves like a global that is hard to discover because it is tucked inside a function or class.  This makes the code harder to understand and can lead to accidental coupling between unrelated parts of the system. | *Best Practices – Global State* (standards_backend_best-practices.md) |
| **Difficult to invalidate** | Since the value is stored in the function’s static context, the only way to “reset” it is to end the request.  Tests that run multiple scenarios in the same request can get stale data, and you cannot easily flush or clear a static cache without re‑initializing the request. | *Best Practices – Global State* |
| **Testing friction** | Unit tests often need isolated, repeatable environments.  Static variables carry over state between tests, meaning you must manually reset or mock them.  This adds boilerplate and makes test failures hard to diagnose. | *Best Practices – Global State* |
| **Concurrency / multi‑thread concerns** | In environments where PHP is run in a multi‑threaded context (e.g., a thread‑pool, or when using parallel execution in tests), static variables are shared across threads, which can cause race conditions or data corruption. | *Best Practices – Global State* |
| **Unintended side‑effects** | A change to a static variable in one part of the code can silently affect any other code that references it.  This makes debugging difficult because the source of the change is not obvious. | *Best Practices – Global State* |
| **Memory consumption** | Static values persist for the duration of the request, even if they are no longer needed.  In long‑running scripts, this can lead to higher memory usage than if the value were local. | *Caching – Runtime Caching* (standards_backend_caching.md) |
| **Hidden dependencies** | Functions that rely on a static variable appear to have no inputs, which hides the dependency and makes refactoring or re‑use harder. | *Best Practices – Global State* |

---

### Practical take‑aways

1. **Prefer explicit parameters or dependency injection** over static variables for values that change per request or per test.  
2. If you need a *runtime cache*, consider using the WordPress object cache layer (`wp_cache_*` functions) or another caching abstraction rather than a plain static variable.  
3. When you do use a static variable, document its purpose and make sure tests clean it up (`static::$var = null;` or `unset(static::$var);`) after each test.  
4. Keep static variables *read‑only* whenever possible, and avoid mutating them after initialization to reduce the risk of side‑effects.

---

**Bottom line:** Static variables create a form of global state that is hard to manage, test, and reason about.  The internal guidelines recommend using them sparingly and only when you have a clear performance or architectural reason that outweighs the disadvantages listed above.

## Runtime Caching
Runtime caching is similar to object caching, but is only stored for a single request. Objects are stored in PHP's memory until the end of the request and are not persisted across requests. (Runtime caching is sometimes called "local" caching.)
The simplest form of runtime caching in PHP is global or static variables. For example, the `$wp_query` and `$post` global variables are runtime caches. Runtime caching is stored entirely in PHP's memory, so it does not incur the latency overhead of hitting an external object cache server.
In WordPress, a runtime cache is built into the object cache layer, which typically ensures good performance for repeated cache lookups, while still using a persistent object cache across all servers. You can also [specifically mark a cache group as non-persistent](https://href.li/?https://developer.wordpress.org/reference/functions/wp_cache_add_non_persistent_groups/), which will turn it into a runtime-only cache.

---

[4] chunk_id: standards_backend_best-practices_chunk_7 | document_id: standards_backend_best-practices
Document: Best Practices > Global State (Category: standards, Source: standards_backend_best-practices.md)

## Global State
Global state is any variable that persists throughout a request. Global state exists both throughout WordPress code and our own code. While global state may be contained in global variables (that is, `$GLOBALS` or `global $var`), it can also exist in other places, including inside object instances.
Where you can, you should reduce global state and ensure it is manageable. Typically, only primary/authoritative data should be stored in global state, while derived data can be regenerated from this. For example, system configuration (like post types) is authoritative, while UI or functionality using those types is derived. Derived data may be [cached](/standards/backend/caching/) (rather than stored) for performance considerations, but consider whether it is worth it first.
You do **not** need to avoid global variables, and often they are a great choice for global state. Using an object property (or static class property) is not necessarily better than a global variable, and can often make testing harder. question: How does `trigger_error()` differ from `error_log()` in terms of functionality?
expected_output:
# Error Logging
With `error_log()` often being used for quick debug output, many code quality tools now flag these calls as forgotten debug statements. This is because `error_log()` is typically used by developers to dump state information directly to the log file, bypassing PHP's error handling system.
A better alternative in many cases is the more versatile `trigger_error()` function. Unlike `error_log()`, it integrates with PHP's standard error handling, respects `error_reporting` and `display_errors`, and is caught by any registered `set_error_handler`. It also supports different error levels, such as `E_USER_NOTICE`, `E_USER_WARNING`, `E_USER_ERROR`, and `E_USER_DEPRECATED`, making it far more expressive than just logging a string.
Additionally, you might come across error messages wrapped in WordPress translation functions. This makes it harder to identify and resolve issues, since bug reports may contain translated messages we can't directly match in the codebase.
End users should not see raw error messages anyway—developers should log or raise errors in a consistent, developer-focused way, and then provide a separate, user-friendly message when needed.
---
agent_answer:
**`trigger_error()` vs. `error_log()` – Core Functional Differences**

| Feature | `trigger_error()` | `error_log()` |
|---------|------------------|---------------|
| **Purpose** | Generates a PHP *user‑level error* that flows through the normal PHP error handling system. | Sends a plain message straight to the configured error log (or a custom log file). |
| **Interaction with PHP error handling** | *Fully integrated* – respects `error_reporting` and `display_errors`, can be caught by a custom `set_error_handler()`. | *Bypasses* PHP’s error handling; it writes to the log directly, so it is not affected by `error_reporting` or a custom handler. |
| **Error levels** | Supports the four user‑defined levels: `E_USER_NOTICE`, `E_USER_WARNING`, `E_USER_ERROR`, `E_USER_DEPRECATED`. These map to standard PHP error levels and can trigger script termination if `E_USER_ERROR` is used. | No error level – it simply logs a string. |
| **Script termination** | If you call `trigger_error(..., E_USER_ERROR)`, PHP will halt execution after the error is handled. | Never terminates the script; it only writes to the log. |
| **Primary use case** | Signalling actual issues in the code (e.g., misuse of an API, deprecated usage, logic errors). Because it behaves like a normal PHP error, developers can handle it consistently, log it, display it, or ignore it based on `error_reporting` settings. | Logging arbitrary diagnostic information, debug traces, or custom messages that should not affect the normal error flow. Often used by developers to dump state for debugging, but can be “forgotten” debug output if left in production. |
| **Typical output** | “Deprecated function used”, “Unexpected value”, etc., with stack trace and file/line context automatically added. | Custom string messages you provide, e.g., “Cache miss for user 42”. |

### Practical Implications

* **Use `trigger_error()`** when you want the error to be part of PHP’s standard error handling pipeline. This lets the rest of the system (error handlers, logging frameworks, production vs. dev configurations) treat it like any other error. It’s also the preferred way for code‑quality tools to flag issues because it provides structured, level‑based information.

* **Use `error_log()`** only when you need to append a raw string to a log file, for example for temporary debugging, telemetry, or when you purposely want to sidestep the error handling flow.

> *From the internal “Error Logging” guide*: “`trigger_error()` integrates with PHP’s standard error handling, respects `error_reporting` and `display_errors`, and is caught by any registered `set_error_handler()`. `error_log()` is a quick debugging tool that bypasses PHP’s error handling system.”

If you’re unsure which to choose, lean towards `trigger_error()` for any situation that represents an actual problem in the code; reserve `error_log()` for non‑error diagnostic output.

## Sanitisation
Validation and sanitisation are two separate but related concepts.
When validating data, you are looking for certain criteria in the data. Or simply put, you're saying "I want the data to have this, this, and this". Sanitisation on the other hand is about removing all the harmful elements from the data. In essence you're saying "I don't want the data to have this, this, and this".
But the difference is more than just conceptual. With validation, we store the data once we have verified it's valid. If not, we discard it.
With sanitisation, we take the data, and remove everything we don't want. This means that we might change the data during the sanitisation process. So in the case of user input, it is not guaranteed that all the input is kept. So it's important that you choose the right sanitisation functions, to keep the data intact.
Refer to the [Sanitisation section of the Security Functions guide](/guides/wordpress/security-functions/#sanitisation) for specific sanitisation functions.

### Namespace and Function Imports
The PHP language allows for functionality to be imported and aliased from external namespaces via the `use` operator in order to avoid writing longer, fully qualified names. It is important to be clear when referencing external functionality so that it is obvious where various functionality is defined. To better distinguish the use of external functionality, the following guidelines should be observed:
* Importing functions explicitly with `use function` should be avoided.
* Aliasing functions explicitly with `use function ... as` should also be avoided.
* Parent namespaces are preferred for importing functions.
* Aliasing namespaces is acceptable, as long as the renaming is kept close to the original. For example `use HM\Block\Helpers as BlockHelpers`
The above are not hard rules, but serve as a general guideline so dependencies
can be easily tracked from within the code.
```
// No:
use function HM\Some\thing;
thing();

// No:
use function HM\Some\thing as other_thing;
other_thing();

// Encouraged:
use HM\Some;
Some\thing();

// Allowed:
use HM\Some\Longer\Namespace as LongerNamespace;
LongerNamespace\thing();
```

WordPress uses three different types of files for managing translations:

question: What is PHPUnit used for in WordPress testing?
expected_output:
# PHPUnit
Writing tests can be tough, especially once WordPress gets involved. Let's do it together.
Most tests you'll work on are written using PHPUnit, so let's work through getting started using PHPUnit. To start with, we're going to work with a very basic PHPUnit test which doesn't load WordPress, and work up to testing a plugin.
You can follow along with the steps here, or clone the repository which includes the parts we're writing here.
If you're using Chassis for local development, you'll want to install the [Tester extension](https://href.li/?https://github.com/Chassis/Tester). This will make PHPUnit available inside your VM, and automatically configure environment variables for WordPress testing.
If you're **not** using Chassis, you need to make sure you have [PHPUnit](https://href.li/?https://phpunit.de/) installed and available on your path.
The first step to getting started is to write a test class. PHPUnit uses class-based tests, which load the class up, then run every method named `test_...()`. If this method runs successfully, the test passes.
agent_answer:
**PHPUnit in WordPress testing**

PHPUnit is the testing framework that WordPress uses for unit‑level tests.  
In the WordPress development workflow, PHPUnit is used to:

1. **Load WordPress into a test environment**  
   - A *bootstrap* file (usually `tests/bootstrap.php`) is configured in `phpunit.xml.dist`.  
   - This bootstrap includes WordPress’ testing framework and sets up the necessary environment variables (`WP_TESTS_DIR`, etc.) so that the full WordPress stack is available during tests.

2. **Run class‑based test suites**  
   - Test classes extend PHPUnit’s `TestCase` and contain methods named `test_*()`.  
   - Each `test_*` method runs automatically; a passing method means the test passes.

3. **Assert expected behaviour**  
   - PHPUnit provides a rich set of assertion methods (`assertEquals`, `assertTrue`, `assertSame`, etc.) to verify that WordPress core, plugins, or themes behave as expected.

4. **Integrate with CI pipelines**  
   - The `phpunit` command can be run in CI (e.g., GitHub Actions, Chassis, etc.) to automatically run the test suite whenever code changes are pushed.

question: What is the main reason for keeping JavaScript hooks separate from styles?
expected_output:
### JavaScript hooks
JavaScript hooks should be kept separate from those used for styles. This allows future developers to move the JavaScript behaviour without the need to modify the CSS.
Our preference is for JavaScript hooks to make use of data attributes, eg `[data-lightbox]`. See the [JavaScript style guide](/how-we-work/style/js/) for further details.
If a JavaScript component must use a class, it should remain separate from styles and be prefixed with `js-`.
agent_answer:
The key reason is to keep the JavaScript behaviour independent of the visual styling.  
From our internal standards:

> **“JavaScript hooks should be kept separate from those used for styles. This allows future developers to move the JavaScript behaviour without the need to modify the CSS.”**  

So by isolating JS hooks (preferably with data attributes or a `js-` prefix) we make it easier to refactor or replace the JavaScript logic later without touching the style sheets. This separation promotes cleaner, more maintainable code.

question: What does the CSS class screen-reader-text explain?
expected_output:
## screen-reader-text class
This class is used to hide content from screen but not from screen readers and search engines.
[The CSS class screen-reader-text](https://href.li/?https://make.wordpress.org/accessibility/handbook/best-practices/markup/the-css-class-screen-reader-text/) explains why and how and gives the most recent CSS properties used for WordPress core.
agent_answer:
**What the `screen‑reader‑text` class explains**

The `screen-reader-text` class is a small CSS snippet that is used throughout WordPress core (and many of its themes) to **hide text from visual display while keeping it available to screen readers and search engines**.  

The documentation explains:

| Why use it | How it works | Typical CSS |
|------------|--------------|--------------|
| You sometimes need to provide a text string that a sighted user shouldn’t see, but a screen‑reader user (or a crawler) should read. | The element is still in the DOM but is taken out of the normal visual flow and clipped so that it is not rendered on the screen. | ```css\n.screen-reader-text {\n  position: absolute;\n  width: 1px;\n  height: 1px;\n  padding: 0;\n  margin: -1px;\n  overflow: hidden;\n  clip: rect(0,0,0,0);\n  white-space: nowrap;\n  border: 0;\n}\n``` |

The documentation also notes that this technique is preferred over using a `<title>` attribute on links for accessibility purposes, as titles are inconsistently supported across devices.  

So, in short, the class **explains that it is a standard, reusable CSS solution for making content invisible to sighted users but still readable by assistive technologies and search engines, and it provides the current set of CSS properties used in WordPress core.**

question: What are the advantages of using a taxonomy to handle one-to-many relationships for posts?
expected_output:
### One to Many Relationships for Posts
When a post needs to be able to be linked to multiple other posts, a possible approach is to use a taxonomy that shadows the post type.
This means that whenever a new post is created, a term in the shadow taxonomy is created. The term name and slug should correspond to the post title and slug, so that display elements and queries can be handled easily.
In practice this means implementing custom create, read, update, and delete functions for the terms in the shadow taxonomy that mimic these operations on posts.
This approach has the advantage that term queries are very fast, and you do not need to worry about any main queries to be impacted.
However the downside here is that posts do support features that taxonomies do not support. Posts can be hidden from the public, but be visible to logged-in users, terms cannot. In addition deleted posts are placed in the trash, whereas terms are deleted immediately.
Whatever your implementation is, it needs to account for this differences in content handling.
agent_answer:
### Why a **taxonomy** (specifically a “shadow” taxonomy that mirrors a post type) is a good fit for one‑to‑many post relationships  

| What it does | Why it’s advantageous |
|--------------|------------------------|
| **Fast term‑based queries** | WordPress stores taxonomy terms in the `term_relationships` table, which is indexed and optimized for quick look‑ups. A query such as “give me all posts that belong to *term X*” runs quickly and doesn’t touch the heavy `wp_posts` table. |
| **No impact on main queries** | Because the relationship lives entirely in the taxonomy tables, the typical `WP_Query` for posts isn’t slowed down by extra JOINs or meta‑queries. The system can keep the normal post‑query path untouched. |
| **Consistent handling of links** | When a post is created, updated, or deleted, you can mirror those operations on its “shadow” term (create the term, update its slug, delete it). This keeps the relationship in sync automatically and leverages WordPress’s built‑in term lifecycle hooks. |
| **Built‑in WordPress functions** | You can use standard taxonomy functions (`wp_set_post_terms`, `get_terms`, `wp_get_post_terms`, etc.) for adding, retrieving, and counting relationships without writing custom database code. |
| **Caching benefits** | WordPress caches taxonomy lookups (`get_the_terms`, `get_terms`) aggressively. This means repeated requests for the same relationship will hit the cache rather than the database, further improving performance. |

**Bottom line:**  
Using a taxonomy to model a one‑to‑many link between posts gives you a **fast, cache‑friendly, and WordPress‑native way** to manage those relationships while keeping your main post queries lean. The trade‑off is that taxonomy terms can’t be hidden from the public in the same way posts can, and deleted terms are removed immediately (not moved to a trash), so you need to account for that in your design.

### Post to Post Relationships for Non-Hierarchical Post Types
When dealing with non-hierarchical posts, the post parent field in the database can be reused for linking entities together. In this scenario, it doesn't matter whether it's a one to one or a one to many relationship.
The limitation here is that there's only one post parent field, so a post can't support multiple relationships this way. In addition the queries on the front end will need to account for this hierarchical relationship.
The *New Post* and *Edit Post* screens in the admin will handle assigning posts to a parent post automatically in the database, as long as a `parent_id` field is sent along in the `$_POST` data when the post is saved. This can be achieved by naming a specific field in your custom UI accordingly.
To retrieve posts, there's the cached `get_children()` function, as well as the `wp_get_post_parent_id()` function. Since hierarchical posts are a built-in WordPress feature, there's support for them in `WP_Query`, and retrieving posts is fast.

### One to One Relationships for Terms and Posts
Another approach is to use object meta to create relationships. This is done by storing the id of the linked entity into a meta field on the entity.
An example might be linking an related post to a video post type. In this scenario, you want the related post to pulled on single video views. You would therefore store the post id in the post meta of the video post type.
It is possible to retrieve the video post type to which a post is linked by doing a meta query. However meta queries are slow, so you would need to implement extra caching if this were used on the front end.

Terms in locked taxonomies should therefore be created in code, preferably during an upgrade routine that only runs once. By doing it this way, the website does not need to implement fallback code for missing terms.
**Hidden** taxonomies go one step further, by not being publicly available. The terms in these taxonomies are only used for retrieving posts. An example for this might be a taxonomy to manage the posts shown in different featured areas on a website.

Document: Architecture > Flat vs. Hierarchical Taxonomies (Category: how-we-work, Source: how-we-work_process_architecture.md)

### Flat vs. Hierarchical Taxonomies
Taxonomies can be divided into main types: **hierarchical** taxonomies and **flat** taxonomies. Which one to use depends a lot on the individual scenario.
Imagine that you have articles that you want to assign to national leagues and football teams. A team can only ever play in one national league. Therefore a straightforward approach might be to have a single taxonomy with parent terms representing the leagues, and child terms for the individual teams. With this approach, it would be easy to list all the teams in a particular league.
At first sight, this is a good solution. However teams do change leagues when they perform well or poorly. So each season you would have to move teams from one league to another, and in the process invalidating a bunch of URLs. So having to flat taxonomies, one for the leagues and one for the teams, would be better. Especially if you add other leagues, like international ones.
The downside is that in this scenario you cannot retrieve the teams in a league easily, because there are no object to object relationships in WordPress.

### Safelisting
The simplest validation method is safelisting. This only works when there is a precise set of possible values that the data can have. These are also sometimes called [enumerated types or enums](https://href.li/?https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enumerated_type).
Let's look at how safelisting can be used for validating a theme option controlling the position of the sidebar.
Here is the code that we used to create the setting and the control:
```
$wp_customize->add_setting( 'sidebar-position', [
    'default'           => 'left',
    'sanitize_callback' => 'hm_validate_sidebar_position',
] );

$wp_customize->add_control( 'sidebar-position-control', [
    'label'    => esc_html__( 'Sidebar Position', 'hm' ),
    'section'  => 'theme',
    'settings' => 'sidebar-position',
    'type'     => 'radio',
    'choices'  => [
        'left' => esc_html__( 'Left', 'hm' ),
        'right' => esc_html__( 'Right', 'hm' ),
    ],
] );
```
The user only has two choices: left or right. This means that in the `hm_validate_sidebar_position()` function, we can determine whether the submitted option is one of the two possible values.

question: How are event handlers defined in the provided example?
expected_output:
### Name event handlers `onEventName`
This is consistent with React's event naming: `onClick`, `onDrag`, `onChange`, etc.
Example:
```
 this.onClick( e ) } onLaunchMissiles={ num => this.onLaunchMissiles( num ) } />
```
```
Component.propTypes = {
    onLaunchMissiles: PropTypes.func.isRequired,
    onScram: PropTypes.func.isRequired,
};
```
agent_answer:
**Event handlers are defined using the `on…` naming convention** – just as React’s built‑in events (e.g., `onClick`, `onChange`, `onDrag`).  

The example from the internal *Standards → React* guide shows the pattern:

```jsx
// Inside a component
this.onClick(e);                     // call an instance method
onLaunchMissiles={num => this.onLaunchMissiles(num)}  // pass a handler to a child

// PropTypes for the handler props
Component.propTypes = {
  onLaunchMissiles: PropTypes.func.isRequired,
  onScram:          PropTypes.func.isRequired,
};
```

**Key points from the example**

| Item | How it’s defined |
|------|------------------|
| **Handler name** | Prefixed with `on` followed by the event name (`onLaunchMissiles`, `onScram`). |
| **Binding** | Handlers can be regular methods (`this.onClick`) or arrow functions passed inline (`num => this.onLaunchMissiles(num)`). |
| **PropTypes** | Declared as required `PropTypes.func` to enforce that a function is supplied. |

So, in the provided example, event handlers are **named with an `on` prefix, passed as props, and typed as `func` in PropTypes**.

### Align and sort HTML properties
Fit them all on the same line if you can. If you can't, put each property on a line of its own, indented one tab, in sorted order. The closing angle brace should be on a line of its own, indented the same as the opening angle brace. This makes it easy to see the props at a glance.
Consistent property ordering makes it easier to manage complex components. Properties should generally be sorted into the following groups, and ordered alphabetically within those groups:
* `key` should be first if required.
* Values
* Event handlers (`on...`)

// Avoid:



 this.onClick() }
    size="40"
/>

// Prefer:


 this.onClick() }
/>
```
Exercise discretion when alphabetising. Alphabetical ordering may not always be the best decision; for example, it may be preferable to keep related positional variables (*e.g.* `height` & `width`) grouped together for clarity.

question: What are the limitations of current state-of-the-art automated testing for frontend accessibility?
expected_output:
## Frontend (DOM) validation
An overview of how to test the DOM for accessibility is given [in the Make WordPress Accessible Handbook](https://href.li/?https://make.wordpress.org/accessibility/handbook/test-for-web-accessibility/test-for-web-accessibility-frontend-code/).
This guide includes checks, tools and resources for:
* Keyboard navigation
* W3C and WCAG 2 AA validation
* Setting up automated testing in the browser and the command line
* Testing dynamic content with a screen reader
As frontend accessibility testing needs to run against the final generated DOM, tests must be run in a full browser. While automated DOM testing does exist, this often requires painful setup. Additionally, current state-of-the-art automated testing does not capture all errors; testing keyboard accessibility and announcing of dynamic changes by a screen reader cannot currently be automated.
agent_answer:
**Short answer**

- Automated tools can check the *generated* DOM against WCAG‑2.0/2.1 rules, but they **cannot** test:
  * real‑world keyboard navigation (tab order, focus management, key shortcuts)
  * how a screen reader announces dynamic content changes (ARIA live regions, updates)
- Running DOM checks in a real browser is still needed, and the setup can be cumbersome.

---

### What the internal documentation says

From the **Accessibility > Frontend (DOM) validation** guide:

> “An overview of how to test the DOM for accessibility … As frontend accessibility testing needs to run against the final generated DOM, tests must be run in a full browser. While automated DOM testing does exist, this often requires painful setup. **Additionally, current state‑of‑the‑art automated testing does not capture all errors; testing keyboard accessibility and announcing of dynamic changes by a screen reader cannot currently be automated.**”

The **Accessibility > Accessibility Testing** guide adds:

> “Testing for accessibility involves a combination of automated testing and manual QA testing. Many of the automated tests are run against the generated content on the site, so depending on the project’s set‑up, may need to be manually run in a browser …”

And the **Testing > Types of Tests** guide summarises:

> “Accessibility testing consists of frontend (DOM) validation, keyboard testing and screen‑reader testing. **DOM validation can be partially automated, while keyboard and screen‑reader testing still needs to be done manually.**”

---

### Key limitations highlighted

| Area | Automated coverage | Current limits |
|------|--------------------|----------------|
| **Static DOM validation** (WCAG‑AA checks, code‑sniffer, axe) | ✔️ | Requires full‑browser rendering; setup can be heavy |
| **Keyboard navigation** (tab order, focus, shortcuts) | ❌ | No reliable automation for real user flows |
| **Screen‑reader behaviour** (ARIA live regions, dynamic updates) | ❌ | Cannot simulate or verify speech output or focus changes |
| **Dynamic content** (React, Vue updates) | ❌ | Automation struggles to capture real‑time state changes |
| **Regression detection** | ✔️ | Only for the aspects the tool can evaluate |

---

### Practical take‑away

If you want to keep CI fast and automated, run a **DOM‑level** tool like **axe** or **HTML_CodeSniffer** against the rendered page.  
For full accessibility confidence you still need:

1. **Manual keyboard checks** – test tab order, focus visibility, key shortcuts.
2. **Manual screen‑reader checks** – verify announcements, live‑region updates, focus changes.

Until tooling advances to reliably emulate a screen‑reader or keyboard session, the combination of automated DOM testing + targeted manual QA remains the best practice.

# Accessibility Testing
Web accessibility aims to create an online space that is available to everyone, and a key part of that is designing websites and software that are flexible for all user needs. It not only helps to deliver content to more people, but small improvements such as the correct semantic use of HTML, CSS and JavaScript will make websites more robust and better prepared for future technologies.
Testing for accessibility involves a combination of automated testing and manual QA testing. Many of the automated tests are run against the generated content on the site, so depending on the project's set up, may need to be manually run in a browser (e.g. [HTML\_CodeSniffer](https://href.li/?http://squizlabs.github.io/HTML_CodeSniffer/)).
The authoritative source for accessibility testing is the [WordPress.org Accessibility Handbook](https://href.li/?https://make.wordpress.org/accessibility/handbook/best-practices/test-for-web-accessibility/), which is maintained by the WordPress Accessibility team. This guide contains a lot more information about accessibility best practices and testing.

## Guidelines
We aim to meet the [WCAG accessibility guidelines](https://href.li/?https://webaim.org/standards/wcag/checklist) at level AA as described in our [frontend best practices](/standards/frontend/best-practices/). Depending on whether a site is being used as a governmental or public service, a different set of legal requirements may apply and this may be a strict requirement.
The Make WordPress Accessible Handbook contains a dedicated section about [Testing for web accessibility](https://href.li/?https://make.wordpress.org/accessibility/handbook/best-practices/test-for-web-accessibility/) with steps and resources.

## Types of Tests
It's important to know that there's many different types of tests you can write. There are some common types we employ though in practice we mostly write integration tests:
* **Integration** tests run a piece of code in the context of the larger application, with services such as databases, cache servers etc…
* **Unit** tests test a single"unit" of your code such as a function. The dependencies of that code would be mocked out (replaced by fake versions) so that it's fully isolated
* **Behavioural or Acceptance** tests simulate user interactions with your application, helpful for preventing regressions in key features
* **Performance** benchmarking is a means of setting a baseline and comparing how well an application or function performs before and after some changes
* **Accessibility** testing consists of frontend (DOM) validation, keyboard testing and screen reader testing. DOM validation can be partially automated, while keyboard and screen reader testing still needs to be done manually.
There are many other types of tests, including visual regression testing. Feel free to explore the other options available to see if anything better suits your project.
